released tuna from the suApic.on cvluUt had hanging over him for so long. When he left the dock the spectators applauded. Outside he was received with cheers. But he didiked all this publicity, and slipped away as speedily as pos- sible to receive the congratulation of Dora and Mrs. Tremewan.

And now, Dora, we can be married," he said, pressing her to his heart. "I am sure I am delighted to hear it," replied Mrs. Tremewan. "Of course I shall miss Dora, who is so dear to me, but you have suffered so much that it is only right you should both have your reward. I for one," with a glance at Mr. Hannaford, ".e ill place no obstacle in the way." "That is very good of you, Mrs. Tremewan," said Harmaford, coolly, "and perhaps your sar- casm is deserved. However, if I was against the marriage then, I am all for it now. I do not desire a more charming or a braver daughter-in- law than Dora. Had it not been for her, I fear the truth would never have come to light." Mrs. Tremewan was not so sure. She had done her best. She had never spared herself, but of course no one gave her the credit she deserved for her courage and toil. She would stay to see Dora married. Certainly. She loved Dora, and wished to see her made happy. She—that is Dora —was leaving a truly happy home. But she— Mrs. Tremewan—trusted that she would have no cause to regret doing so. Marriage was a lottery, and certainly she had been very happy herself with Mr. Tremewan. Of course she had been an exceptionally good wife to him, but she was thankful to say that he was one of the few men who_could appreciate a woman's devotion. As to Walter Pillage, he was certainly a villain—" One of the worst, I should say," put. in Mr. Hannaford, sharply. Mrs. Tremewan quite agreed. No words were too bad for the man. To have deceived her, and to have come into her when she thought he was dead and buried. It was really very pain- ful. No one knew what she had felt. But then she was so much more sensitive than other people. However, Pillage had gone away without taking leave of anyone save of that creature Ellen Jinney. Mrs. Tremewan believed the creature kept a low public-house----" "Don't be too hard on her." pleaded Will., 'Mit for Miss Jinney that omafession would never have been obtained.'

Mrs. Tremewan was glad to hear that Ellen Jitney had done some good. .At one time she believed Walter had been attracted to her. She (Mrs. Tremewan) was thankful that such a vile man was not her husband after all. He really ought to marry Miss Jinney after what had passed. Miss Jamey had saved Walter's life-' "Well, mother, perhaps he will marry her for doing so." "No, Dora. I beg your pardon. I know all about it. Walter has gone to America in that boat of his, and has taken with him that dread- ful =aloe who never left him. I did hear that Walter promised to send for Ellen Jimmy when he made his fortune, but that is what he promised me when he left for England. A bad man, Dora I..Ast us hope he will mend." All this and much more Mrs. Tremewan said, regarding herself as a martyr. She was present at the marriage of Dora, and wept the whole time because of her daughter's loss. Considering the way in which she had neglected the girl, this at- titude made those who knew wonder at her blind- ness. But the majority of the guests said that it was very sweet of dear Mrs. Tremewan to feel the loss so much, and that she was a dear little woman, who had led a most unhappy life. On the whole therefore the widow was pitied and praised quite as much as she desired. After the marriage she left for the Continent,. "I really must go to Switzerland to see if my nerves will recover after the various shocks I have undergone," she said. Fortunately I have a good income and a faithful and devoted maid. I feel greatly the troubles I have had. But we must all be resigned. Although I will say that if Dora had only understood me, I should not have suffered so much. But she never did com- prehend suffering; Dora had no nerves. Abso- lutely none." With this farewell Mrs. Tremewan took her de- parture. She intended to go to Switzerland, but halted at Paris. Finding the gay city much to her taste, and having some introductions, she re- mained there. The last time Dora and Will heard of her she was not disinclined to marry for the third time.

"And she will give her new husband all the property," said Will. "Do you mind?" asked Dora; "for my part I am not sorry. "No more am I," replied her husband. "Any- thing which has to do with the Tremewan pro- perty puts my teeth on edge." Vane was of course much disappointed that he lost the estates, but he consoled himself with the reflection that he had saved his neck. But for the confession of Mrs. Bedowen it is hard to say what might have happened. So Vane poor in purse, but safe in person, returned to London a sadder and a wiser man. Since he had suffered. somewhat, Will Haiinaford spared him the thrash- ing he so richly deserved for his freak about the rope. Some six months after the marriage of Will and Dora Sue Gillard came to see her friend. Young Mrs. Har.naford was living with her father-in- law, for he was so attached to her that he could not bear her out of his sight. "Dora," said Sue, who looked rosy and de- lighted, "he has proposed!" "Dr. Pasco, dear? Of course I knew he would." "Well, Dora, of course I knew that he loved me. But then I thought my parents—at least one of them—might be a bar to his entertaining any ideas of matrimony. But he proposed, and I said yes, and be has seen father " "What does your father say?" "He was angry at first. But when Jack—l call him Jack now," said Sue, with another blush, "promised to settle something on me and help the boys to get into the army, and assist father to arrange his affairs, (Tear father gave way! Oh, what a savage parent!" sighed Sue. "Never mind, dear. You will soon have a home of your own."

"Thank goodness!" cried Miss Gillard, piously-. "But it does seem hard that father should spoil love's young dream with questions about money. Jack is well off though, MO that is all right. Tom is to go to a tutors, and afterwards to Sand- hurst. It will be all right-" "And you will be Mrs. Pascoe," said Dora, kissing her. "Well, dear, I only hope you will be as happy as I am." " I am sure you deserve your happiness, Dora," cried Sue, giving her an affectionate hug, "after all the trouble you have had. That horrid house- keeper! Remember how I said she could scratch." "Hush, darling. I want to forget all that 11114 happy time." "Well, I'm sure I don't want to bring it back to you," said Sue, "and-" "What are you two talking about?" asked Will, entering at this moment. Dora explained, and Will congratulated Sue. When the girl was gone he turned to his wife. "Miss Jinney has sold The Eight Bells, and has gone to America. I can't learn the precis* locality." "She has gone to marry Pillage." "I can't say. But she has gone bag and baggage. If the man is not an absolute scoundrel he certainly ought to marry her. She saved his life. My wonder is that she has the courage to go to him." - • "There is some good in him, and-" "No, Pora. There is no good in the man. He is a scoundrel, and as for Mrs. Bedowen-"

"Hush, Will. She is dead. Say no more. Let us talk of your new book." Will laughed, and they began to talk of his novel which .was to make him famous. Dora thought it a work of genius, and even the elder Hannaford approved of it in his dry way. But he always said when his criticism was ended:— "Say what you like, Will, but you will never find in your brain a more exciting story than your own. Mrs. Bedowen aa a heroine would be a capital character." "She would," assented Will, "but not sympa- thetic. However, I agree with you. Fact has certainly been poaching on the domain of fiction. If the public knew the tale—" "They would not believe it," said Mr. Hanna, ford. "However, the story has ended as excel- lently in real life as it could have done in fiction."
"With wedding bells," said Dora,. kissing her husband. After which they spoke of themselves, and left Mrs. Bedowen's name to the oblivion her wickedness deserved.

div.head: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
div.p: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

The fine weather has been the cause of the appearance of a bewildering number of dainty toilettes and hats, The prolongation of the rainy season has up till now created great discontent in many feminine bosoms, for the many delicate-toned and fancifully- trimmed toilettes selected for • early spring were consequently condemned to repose un- folded in the seclusion of folds of tissue paper, At last has come the opportunity to display the triumphs of taste and modistic skill to the admiring eyes of all beholders,

The prevailing Modes at the present time are, it must be confessed, merely an accentua- tion of the leading styles of eally spring, and only serve to emphasise the fact that skirts are fuller and more trimmed, belts deeper and more pronounced in outline, while shoulder capes and boleros become so similar that it is well-nigh impossible to distinguish the one from the other. Colours are dis- tinctly of the pale order, and the most popular for afternoon toilettes are white,
A PRETTY TOILETTE. champagne, and silver and oyster

The pretty toilette depicted is of tussore silk trimmed with lace and lace insertion, and is very modish worn with a burnt straw hat of a picturesque style. Tussore colour far more clearly defines the most fashionable colour for this season than any other, as it is a happy medium between yellow and string colour, and it offers an excellent background for showing off the rich embroideries so much worn. White and ivory appliques also stand out well against it, while floral brocadings appear at • their bvt, and the effect of all sorts of lace is most charming. The 'bolero still reigns supreme in every department of dress, whether tailor-made or of the more airy, fairy description, and the most popular form of this little garment this season is a sort of semi-cape which is easily slipped off and on, and which gives a finished look to an afternoon or visiting toilette which is otherwise wanttng. Somehow, when in town on business or pleasure bent, a coat or cape seems a neces- sary complement of dress, and from this want arose the popularity of the neck ruffle, which ..has .now increased so in size and ha-

portance as to merit the title of cape, These dainty adjuncts of dress are made with many fussy frills .round the shoulders, while long stole ends depend down the - front to the knees.

The .cape .bolero, however, as shown in my innovation, is of sa. simpler description, and clearly defines the line of the shoulders and throat.. This will be appreciated by all those whom nature has dowered with a graceful figure, while :the more fussy neck ruffle can be substituted when any softening of angular outlines is of ,advantage. • It is the woman who knows just what kind of garment to select to best suit her own style of face and figure who will always merit the title of being well dressed, whether her gown be of a costly or cheap material. Feather boas are also much in vogue as a finish to a toilette, and a handsome white ostrich feather boa is certainly very becoming. Among the many lovely materials for summer wear will .be found some very fine French lawns and batistes richly embroidered in raised white Swiss work, which contrasts well against the backgrounds of blue, mauve, -.or pink, and make up into very charming toilettes. The prettiest are those which are simply made with the lower half of the skirt -plissé, while the upper -part, which is gauged at the waist, is formed of the embroidery.

div.p: A SUMMER HAT.
The'bodem has the yoke and upper part of the sleeves finely tucked, while the remainder. -which simulates a bolero, is of the embroidery, a wide bend holding in the fulness at the

The pretty hat depicted is for summer wear, and is of rustic straw trimmed with ribbon, The shape is of the plateau order, and a knot of lace at the back forms a small cache-peigne. The cache-peive is not so prominent a 4eature in millinery as it was some six months ago, but it still adds grace to certain •models. Occasionally it is re- placed by ribbon strings, which, coming from the back of the hat, are knotted in a bow and ends underneath the hair behind. To achieve success, however, the hair must be dressed half-way. down the back of the head. Belts for the waist are becoming quite one of the leading features of a costume, and one of the newest and most fanciful styles is made of plaited straw and is about a couple of inches wide. These are, of course, very light and cool to wear, but are not, to my mind, so smart as the patent leather belts in emerald green or black, which are in- visibly perforated to allow of ventilation, This, of course, is necessary if one is taking much exercise, There are also some ex- ceedingly pretty suede belts, which are slightly draped, and are fastened in front by ornamental buckles, These belts are very supple, and At the figure to perfectioni COQ tacrral

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The number of fashionable weddings that were I solemnised last month would seem to show that the old I idea that ill-luck follows the May bride is going the way of most of the legends of May. There was the old belief which has prevailed for centuries., that washing the face in May dew gave beauty, but we hear very little of this old custom now. Another ancient practice associated with May, and employed by rustic folks, was 1 _ _ _ _
that of divining thi;luturp from snails, the track tieing

examined to foi-m letters in answer to questions put, iii much the same way as the writing of the planchetta. ' These as well as most of the rites and revelries of May, have all but disappeared, even in our villages, and, to judge from the number of weddings announced last month, the old superstition against May matriages, is • losing much of its force in fashionable society. The report on the census of 1901, which has just been published discloses the extraordinary fact that there aro twice as many widows as there are widowers in , England and Wales, though the number of unmarried and married personsof bah sexes is about the same. These figures would appear to show that the widow—all designing as she is supposed to be—is not nearly so fortunate in marrying again as is the widower, but possibly the deativrate has a good deal to do with the great disproportion disclosed in the summary tables. Some men would account for the large number of "superfluous women" by suggesting that it is the "poor husband." who gets worried to death, but it would probably be much nearer the truth to say that men do not live so long as women because they are more addicted to living upon the principle of a short life and a merry one. In any case it would appear that the preference which the insurance offices give to the life of a married woman, over that of a married man, is

div.head: NIGHT
div.p: THE NIGHT
The Examiner Friday, June 5, 1903.

"That won't do," said 'Tom, speaking for the first time; "we saw her by the dead body." "Ah!" Mrs. Bedowen was down on the flaw. "Then you did not see me commit the murder ae you say?" "Toni did not. He arrived late. But I saw you throw the cord over Mr. Tremewan's head." Mrs. Bedowen tried to smile and failed. "Mere raving," she said, with a twisted lip, and thought how she could escape. "I daresay you killed the man yourself, or at least assisted Pillage to do so. Yes," she rose triumphant, "you did. You came with Pi11:1.2.e from the inn. ho you think I don't know that he was about the house? I saw him in the light which streamed from the study win- dow-. I was at an upper window, and I recognised him. No deedvirg me. I have eyes like a cat. I can in the dark—almost. Pillage was there. I did not see you—his accomplices—but by your own confes,ion you were there. Ha!" cried the woman, dapping her hands, "I shall go to Dartbridge to-morrow and add a line to my affi- davit. Pillnese killed Tremewan, assisted by you two. A triple hanging," she jeered. Even Ally:. Jinney's nerves gave way before this malignaacy. " What a real devil you are!" she said, faintly, and chin.; to Tom.

"Then don't rouse -me," cried Mrs. Bedowen, seeing her advantage. "Here are two doors. One leads out to the front through the passage, the other to the back through the kitchen. You can take whatever way you like, but," she flung her- self forward fiercely, "leave my house!" "Hold up," whispered Tom to his companion; "it's for the master's sake."

"Leave my house," repeated Mrs. Bedowen. "All in good time," said Tom, heavily. "Your temper may frighten her," and he pointed with his thumb to Miss Jinney, "but it don't matter a. peat to me. Hold your tongue, or I'll knock you, down.".

"Do you think I care? I hare beaten many a better man than you," and Mrs. Bedowen snapped her fingers, with an infernal look of rage. "Wait! Wait!" cried Miss Jinney, flinging herself between them. "If you wish to escape hanging, listen." "I am in no danger of being hanged," raved the other. "You are," Mies Jinney stamped. "Be silent and listen,' she cried. "When Mr. Pillage left the house, Tom, who slept at his door, overheard him go out. He woke me, as he feared Mr. Pillage might get into trouble. We followed, but lost him. After some wandering I suggested that he might have gone after you. We therefore went to The Gray House. He was not there. But we saw you through the window of the study talking to Mr. Tremewan. You were raging at him. Then you turned to leave the rooni. Mr. Tremewan turned to his desk. You darted back as you saw that he was off his guard, and threw the cord over his neck. We saw you with our own eyes struggle with him. He flung up his hands, and his face grew black. He was dead in less than a minute. You did your work well. Then you arranged his hands on the desk, and slipped out of the room, leaving the window open and the lamp burning. We were too horrified to interfere. When you had gone we saw Mr. Pillage enter the room by the window. When he found the dead body he seemed startled, and hurriedly went away. Tom and I got back to the inn as quick as we could. Mr. Pillage never knew we had been out. We never said anything of this to him. We spoke of your wickedness to no one, for we were afraid lest Mr. Pillage also—having been on the spot—should get into trouble. But now you have accused him, we come forward to tell the truth. You com- mitted the crime, and you must write out a con- fession. Tom and I will be the witnesses—"

_ "And if I refuse?" said Mrs. Bedowen, with white lips. "We will have you arrested at once. Tom will stay here, and I'll go for the polioe." "And if I give you the confession?" Miss Jinney shrugged her shoulders. "We'll give it to Mr. Pillage, and he can do what he likes."

Mrs. Bedowen thought. There was a chance of escape then, although but a faint one. If she wrote out the confession, she knew that it would pass by the fidelity of these two faithful creatures into her husband's possession. She might then see him, and beg him to give her a chance of getting out of the country. He was her husband after all, and he might even give her his yacht to fly in. Certainly she .had not deserved well of him, and he might give her up; but there was a chance that he would relent. Besides she was between the devil and the deep sea—Walter Pillage being the devil. Either she must give the confession and trust to her husband's generosity, or she must refuse and be arrested at once. The last alternative was not to be thought of. In the face of these witnesses she could offer no defence. She therefore took the only course open to her. "I'll sign a confession," said Mrs. Bedowen. "And write it out!" cried Miss Jinney. must say why you killed the man." "I don't mind. Wait till I get the ink and paper." • Tom placed his back against the inner door. "You don't leave this room," he said. "I see pen and paper over there." Mrs. Bedowen gave him a look of white fury, and smiled blandly. "How forgetful of me!" she said, going to the place indicated. "I declare you are right !" She brought the writing materials to the table. "I will make the confes- sion as short as possible." She sat down. "I can depend upon your giving it to my—to Pillage?"
"You

"Yes," said Miss Jinney, shortly, "you can." Mrs. Bedowen wasted no more time. She took up the pen and began to write, but slowly, not being an accomplished scribe. Miss Jinney looked over her shoulder, and occasionally assisted her in the spelling of a word, while Tom leaned against the inner door whieh led into the kitchen. The outer door leading to the passage was ajar, and owing to that circumstance they could hear the rain very plainly. It was beating hard on the roof. Mrs. Bedowen took some time, but in due season the confession was finished, and squar- ing her elbows, she read it out to Tom, the other woman still looking over her shoulder. ill was done quite methodically. The self-command of the terrible housekeeper was marvellous. Yet she knew that failing the pity and connivance of her husband she was absolutely lost. "I, Judith Bedowen," read the housekeeper, "hereby state that I alone murdered my master, Francis Trernewan, on the night of the fifteenth of January. I saw that he was anxious before I retired to bed, and determined to learn what was the matter. I came down the stair i and listened at the study door, as I heard voices within. I heard Mr. Will Hannaford tell to my master a secret which I thought was mine alone. Mr. Will asked my master to alter his will so that things might be right for his wife and daughter. My master agreed to do this, and added that he would cut my name out of the will. I was down for an annuity of two hundred a year, and I was de- termined not to lose it. Some time after Mr. Will had left I walked in and told my master what -I had heard. He was angry with me, and said that he would certainly cut my name out of the will, and make a new one. I implored him not to leave me penniless. But he showed no mercy, and said many cruel things to me. I then made U p my mind to kill him before he could make a fresh will. On pretence of arranging the curtains I obtained the cord of one of them. I feigned to depart after making one last attempt to soften Mr. Tremewan. He declined to listen, so when he turned again to the desk I threw the cord over his head and strangled him. He suffered very little. I then went to bed and gave the alarm next morning myself. I may also state. that I wrongfully accused Mr. Pillage. He is absolutely innocent I killed Francis Tremewan, and for the above reason. lam not at all sorry for what I have done. He was going to 'cheat me, and he deserved his fate. (Signed) • "Judith Bedowen." Such was the document, although the spelling has been amended. Tom and Miss Jinney both sinned as witnesses, the latter taking charge of the precious document. Mrs. Bedowen, pale, but still composed, rose to take leave of her nit:7 welcome visitors.

"Now that you have done your worst," she said, savagely, "I hope you will do me the honour of leaving my house." As she spoke she crossed over to the outer door and laid her hand on the handle. At that moment Tom, after a glance at Miss Jinney, knocked at the inner door. It opened, and Inspector Tait appeared. Mrs. Bedowen gasped. "Here is the confession," said Miss Jinney, giving it to the Inspector. "You heard it read?" "Yes," replied Tait, slowly. arrest her."
"I am ready to

fury ana nes-pair—sne openen rue noor tia away before they could stop her. With an ex- clamation Tait followed. But the fugitive was already out of the house and had vanished into darkness. The Inspector rushed blindly forward and shouted to his subordinates—who were wait- ing in the kitchen—to come out. _ .

-Meantime Mrs. Bedowen had cleverly thrown them off the scent. Instead of going round by the gate and out on to the high road as Tait expected, she had climbed over the low wall directly in front of her house, and in spite of her weight, had lowered herself by clinging to the bushes. Below was the water, and here she hoped to find a boat. It was her idea to row her- self out to the yacht, and there remain in hiding until Pillage arrived. The police would never think of looking for her there—in the very jaws of the lion, as it were. The plan had oc- curred to her immediately she had recognised her danger. And the gloom, the rain, and her own infernal ingenuity enabled her to carry it into effect.

"Everything lost," she muttered, as she dropped down on the shingle, for even in the midst of her alarms her brain was clear; "all I have fought for gone. My cottage, my annuity. I am in a worse way than I was when I tramped from Haggardton. Shall I ever eat well and sleep soft again? Curses on those who betrayed me!"

She was not at all sorry for her own guilt. She pitied herself profoundly. To be betrayed at the eleventh hour—to lose all. It was desperately hard. Mrs. Bedowen could have wept for her sufferings, but she had no time. Her present safety had to be thought of. Unexpectedly a light appeared above. It was a lantern lowered by one of the policeman. Not finding her on the high road, Tait guessed that she might have taken flight by dropping over the cliff. Mrs. Bedowen pressed herself close to the rocks in the hope of escaping notice. In this she was successful, and the light was drawn up. This good fortune cheered her. She thought she, would yet get the better of he enemies, and crept out to the rocks, where she hoped to find a boat. It occurred to her that the day before she had noticed one anchored immediatedy below her house. If she could only find it 1. The gloom was profound and the rain poured down steadily. With her bare head and un- covered shoulders Mrs. Bedowen, more wretched than she had ever been in the whole of her wicked life' stumbled down to the water's edge. She fancied she saw the boat some little distance out, near a rock. It was high tide, and she found nerself up to her knees in water. But she cared very little for this, as she was already wet to the skin. She must escape at all costs. The gallows awaited her if she failed.

Across the shingle, knee-deep in the water, over the black, hard rocks, she plunged in the gloom. At times she fell; her hands were cut and bleed- ing, she ached in every bane, and her brain was on fire with terror and anguish. She saw the boat. There it swung with the tide, moored to a rock some distance away. A channel of swirling water divided her from the little craft. She leaped from one rock to another, sometimes miss- ing her footing, but always contriving to regain it with the activity of a cat. More lights appeared above. One began to drop to the lower level. There was no time to be lost. With a great effort she tried to leap the last channel of water which cut her off from the boat. Gathering herself together for a final effort, she jumped—and missed her footing. The next instant she was plunged in the water. This was the end. She could not swim. She had lost her clear head. Like a stone she dropped to the bottom. She rose again. She clutched hopelessly at the rock as she was whirled past by the strong gush of water. Her fingers missed. She grasped at the boat. It swung away at her touch. She tried to cry out, for the fear of death was upon her. But the water filled her mouth. Again she went down. Her gar- ments, all soaking with sea water, dragged her to perdition. The strong tide caught her in its grasp and swept her away from the land. Above was the black sky, below the greedy water, and between the two this wretched creature fighting desperately for her life. At length the end came. She gave one wild cry which startled those who searched for her—and then went down. The waters closed over her head. She was no more a living woman. Overtaken not by the punish- ment of man, but by the judgment of God, the woman who had robbed, had murdered, had sinned in every way vanished from the world she had disgraced and afflicted.

div.head: CLERGYMAN ON HAPPINESS.
div.p: A CLERGYMAN ON HAPPINESS.
CHAPTER XXV,
CALM AFTER STORM.

With the confession and death of Mrs. Bedowen the mystery of Tremewan's murder came to an end. In the most handsome manner Inspector Tait acknowledged to Mr. Hannaford and his son that he had been utterly wrong. "But, of course," he said, "I don't pretend to be a detective of fiction. In real life we are all liable to make mistakes. You must forgive my official zeal, Mr. Will."
"Oh, now that. it is all over I forgive you, answered Will, with a shrug. "By the way, Tait, how much of this business .do you know?" _ _

"I don't understand, sir." "I mean, what did Mrs. Bedowen and Mr. Pillage tell you?" 'A great deal," replied Tait, significantly. "I know that Mr. Pillage is the husband of Mrs. Tremewan, and that Mrs. Bedowen blackmailed her master on account of the secret. _ She murdered him—if you will read the confession— because he was about to cut her out of his will. I suppose, sir," he added, turning to the elder Hannaford, "that the estate will go to Mr. Vane. But Miss Tremewan—"

"She will marry my son," said Mr. Hannaford. "I hope no other outside person knows these details, Inspector." "No one else knows, sir. And I will keep my mouth shut, you may be sure. In the confession Mrs. Bedowen does not explain the secret, so when it is produced at your trial, Mr. Will, very little need be said."
"I must stand my trial, F suppose?" "Certainly. But it will be a mere matter of form, sir. We will keep this painful family history to ourselves. I believe Mr. Pillage is only too anxious to do so."

"I don't wonder at it, considering the part he played," said Mr. Hannaford, sharply. "I thought that Pillage, whatever his faults, was a gentleman. At least he was when I knew him many years ago. I expect his association with Mrs. Bedowen corrupted his manners." "Ahi She was a bad lot, sir. Well, she has met with her deserts, and for the preservation of this family matter it is just as well that she was not brought to trial."
"Had her body been found, Tait?" "No, Mr. Will. I don't think it ever will. I believe the tide carried it out to sea. We'll never see her again alive or dead."
"Just a well;" replied Will. "By the way, Tait, you are wrong on one point. Pillage is not the husband of Mrs. Tremewan."

Tait looked astonished. "Why, sir, it was 'on that account-" "Yes! Yes! Tremewan was blackmailed be- cause he believed that. But it seems that before Pillage married Mrs. Tremewan he was already the husband of Mrs. Bedowen."
- "Do you mean to say he was married to her, air?"
" Yes, Ido say so. He is as bad as her, and I wish he could be punished. But for the sake •of all we will let him go." "Well!" Inspector Tait could only look amazed.

"So you see, Tait," put in Mr. Hannaford, en- joying the confusion, Mrs. Tremewan is after all the legal wife of her late husband—the second, as you may say. She keeps the estates, and the will stands. Mr. Vane will have to go without the property." "And serve him right!" cried Will. "I am not vindictive, but upon my word when I think how near he was killing me with that rope—" "Yon can prosecute him if you like, Mr. Will." "No. The loss of the property will be punish- ment enough." For some time the trio talked over the matter. Then the Inspector took his leave, much humbled in his own opinion. A plain murder of the ordinary sort he could understand, but this mystery was above the grasp of his intelligence. "But thank heaven," said Tait, as he wended his way to the police-office, "I am not likely to have anything mere of this sort. I'd rather read about it in a Lovel, than have to do with it in real life." _ _

div.head: EVENTS OF THE WEEK
div.p: EVENTS OF THE WEEK
LORD ONSLOW'S SUCCESSOR.

When Lord Onslow was promoted to the 'aloard of Agriculture it was prophesied upon •every side that he would be succeeded as Under-Secretary of State for the Colonies by Lord Monk Bretton, and the choice gives general satisfaction, as the young peer is a very popular man in politics. For the last two years he has been acting as principalprivate secretary to Mr. Chamberlain, and therefore has the work of his new office at his fingers' ends. Thus his quail& cation is un- loubted, which s a great thing in a political appointment. He accompanied the Colonial Sec- retary on his famous tour of South Africa, MONK BRETTON. and has been with- him through a considerable part of the trying time of the recent war. Lord Monk Bretton is young for office, being only thirty-three; but he has been in "training" practically ever since his Eton and Oxford days. He suc- ceeded to the peerage in • 1897, and owns about four thousand acres in Sussex: His lather, the first peer, was a well-known poli- tician, first as Mr. Dodson, and then as Lord *Monk Bretton, being raised to the peerage in 1884. He served various offices, such as Deputy Speaker of the House of Commons, Financial Secretary to the Treasury, Presi- dent of the Local Government Board, and Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster. From this it will be seen that the new Under-Secre- tary for the Colonies was bred and brought up 'in the atmosphere of politics.

div.head: PROMISING AIRSHIP.
div.p: A PROMISING AIRSHIP.

Two famous experimentists in wrial navi- gation, MM. Julliot and Surcouf, have suc- ceeded in making an airship which is expected to establish records. This car, which has been named the Lebandy, is considerably different from any of those designed by Santos Dumont. or, for that matter, by anybody. The prin- ciple, howpver, of elevation is the same, a hydrogen balloon being employed, though this is much longer and narrower than that of Dumont's latest ship, and admits of the vessel being more easily navigated. It has been said that no really efficient airship can be con- structed that relies on an inflated bag for elevation, and that so long as the balloon element exists so long will wrial navigation remain in an experimental state. There does not, however, at the moment seem any pro- 'bability of the balloon being dispensed with,
which was built on the Wear, has an odd ap- pearance owing to her extraordinary number of masts. However, she is not a sailing ship, b- steam,- if 2,200 h.p. with a speed of

div.head: LEBAUDY DIRIGIBLE AIRSHIP;
div.p: THE LEBAUDY DIRIGIBLE AIRSHIP;

.and all efforts for the time being seem to be directed to making the balloon as dirigible as possible. In being so much narrower than any ,other, the Lebaudy balloon is, of course, first in this respect, some really remarkable feats of stgering having been performed with it. The locomotion is effected by a two-bladed Propeller on each side of the car in the middle, and the motive power is by means of very efficient gasoline engines. The Lebaudy has the disadvantage, at any rate in its pre- sent state, of being a somewhat dangerous Ship to handle, but its dcsig,ners are confident of making it a perfectly safe vessel when they have effected the improvements they have in mind. In fact, MM. Julliot and Surcouf have mow announced their readiness to attempt the journey from Moisson to Mantes and 'back:

div.head: NOVEL POLAR EXPEDITION.
div.p: A NOVEL POLAR EXPEDITION.

In these days, when Arctic exploration is carried on at great expense in or from well- fortified steamships fitted with all modern requirements and much comparative luxury, it is refreshing to find a man who, following the example of Frobisher and Davis, and other daring seafarers. intends to set out on a scienti- fic venture to the North Mag- netic Pole in a little sloop of , some 46 tons register. Cap- tain Roald Amundsen, the leader of the expedition, is a Norwegian mas- ter mariner, of , considerable Arctic and Ant- artic experience, as well as much scientific know- ledge, gained on voyages to the Greenland seas, ta.nd as chief CAPTAIN ROALD AMUNDSEN. officer of the Melgicas, under command of Captain de iGerlache, to the Antartic waters south of the liorni For his present purpose he has pur- chased an ordinary, stoutly built Norwegian walrus sloop, the GjOa, which he has had fortified, and fitted with a petroleum engine, which, under favourable conditions, can propel Ihe Ivessel at a speed of four knots. The estimated cost of the expedition is L 5. s°o. a great part being defrayed by Captain Amund- sen himself, the rest by contributions from the t King of Norway and Sweden, the Royal Geographical Society, and various private Persons. The party, in addition to the leader, consists of, Lieutenant Gotfred Hansen, Royal Danish Navy, second in command, and six Other men.

div.head: REVOLUTION IN DREDGING.
div.p: THE REVOLUTION IN DREDGING.

r The new ship Grangesberg, of which we give a picture, odd as she may appear at first Sight, promises,. if she proves a success, to create a revolution in the shipping world. She has been built with a view to swiftness of unloading; and whereas in the ordinary Way it would take a fortnight, it is expected that with her novel appliances she will be Itmptied of her cargo in thirty hours. If the Ship of the future can be unloaded in a day or two days, instead of a week or fortnight, ItIS obvious that an enormous increase in °e-ean-borne cargo will be the natural result to the great benefit not only of shipping but of commerce generally. The Grangesberg,

tion has by now been completed, and a private concession has been granted to a company to carry out the installation of a large power plant at the famous Victoria Falls on the Zambesi, which were discovered and named by Livingstone in 1855. The water will be used in a similar manner to the power plants at Niagara, but the Victoria Falls are more than twice the width and double the height of the celebrated American Falls. It is esti- mated that an average horse-power of thirty- five millions will be obtained, and this in the heart of Africa will be of inestimable value and an immense' aid to civilisation.
THE BRIDGE TO BE _ ERECTED OVER THO ZAISESI AT THE VICTORIA FALLS

div.head: R. LE HUNT
div.p: R. LE HUNT

on his appoint- ment. Just over fifty years of age, Mr. Le Hunte has served in many important positions in the Colonies since he came down from Cambridge. He was first Secretary to Sir A. Gordon (Lord Stanmore), the first Governor of Fiji, and filled many offices out there. In 1887 Mr. Le Hunte was appointed President of Dominica, and seven years later he went on to Barbadoes as Colonial Secretary. In 1897 he went to Mauritius in the same capacity, and a year later he became Lieutenant Governor of New Guinea. His latest promotion is his appoint- ment to South Australia.

div.head: MOTOR FIRE ENGINES.
div.p: MOTOR FIRE ENGINES.

There is every likelihood of the motor fire engine becoming general in England. The one now on trial at Battersea is giving the great- est satisfaction. It is propelled by steam, and when running to a fire, is capable of attaining a speed of 30 miles per hour. Because of its short wheel base, it can turn in less than 20 feet. The steering pivots are in the centre of the hubs, in order to make the machine steer easily. A single boiler, of the vertical fire tube type, supplies steam for both the

div.head: NEW LONDON MOTOR FIRE ENGINE.
div.p: THE NEW LONDON MOTOR FIRE ENGINE.

propelling and pumping engines, the former of which is of 25 horse power. The general arrangement and method of control can be se?n at a glance from the illustration. The controlling levers are at the front, and the engineer simply attends to the boiler, which is tired by petroleum instead of coal. The machine was built at the headquarters of the Brigade at Southwark, and will doubtless be followed by other vehicles after it has had a sufficiently thorough testing to have shows its

div.head: SOUTH AUSTRALIA'S NEW GOVERNOR.
div.p: SOUTH AUSTRALIA'S NEW GOVERNOR.

Since the States of Australia were federated and a Governor-General installed, naturally the position of the individual Governors is not one of so much importance, either socially or politically, and the Colonial Office are sending out a different type of man. The new Govern.

ors are now rather men who have made their way to the top of the public service—not simply peers: Such a man is Mr. George Ruthven Le Hunte, who has been decorated for his many Colonial ser- vices, and South Australia, which has hitherto been directly the province of Lord Tennyson, the Governor- Gene- ral, is to be congratulated

On Saturday, a handicap at bowls for Mr. E. T. Evans' annual prize took place on the Viaduct Insti- tute green: There were 40 entries, and some good bowling was witnessed, the green being in excellent condition. Thewinners were :-1, S. Thompson; 2, W. Keening; 3, Joseph Spencer.
INTER-WORKS CUP COMPETITION. THE FIRST ROUND.

Three more matches tn the first round of this com- petition were played on the green of the King and Queen, Padgate, on Saturday. Ideal weather prevailed. Considerable interest has been aroused in the competi- tion, and it prontises to be a great success. The most keenly contested match was that between Orford Tannery and Stubbs' File Works, the issue lying in the balance until the last woods had been bowled.

div.head: WHITSUNTIDE HOLIDAY.
div.p: THE WHITSUNTIDE HOLIDAY.

Nowhere is a relaxation from the daily round of toil, i however brief, more appreciated than n busy centres I of industry such as Warrington and Warrington people can always be relied upon to make the most of oppor- tunities of quitting the grimy town and betaking them- selves to rural or seaside haunts. The Whitsuntide holiday was anticipated with additional pleasure be- • cause the glorious weather of last week gave rise to sanguine hopes that the conditions during the week-end would be admirably conducive to holiday making. • Happily these hopes were fully realized: The rain of Friday had the effect of laying the dust and reviving vegetation, and cyclists looked ' forward to a happy time on the morrow. Saturday morning broke somewhat unpromisingly but during the forenoon the clouds rolled away and ifor the remainder of the day there was brilliant sun- • ahine. On Sunday the *weather was ideal and in the afternoon the Park was thronged with people who desired to hear the band performance. Whitsunday is observed as one of the greatest festivals of the year in the Anglican and Roman Catholic Churches, and on Sunday the services partook ajoyous character befitting the occasion. Many of the churches were prettily decorated with flowers and greenery. During the night the weather prospects underwent a change, and on Monday morning a dull grey sky and a chilling breeze gave promise of ram later in the day. At noon however, the wind changed quarter, the sun emerged from the clouds, and for the rest of the day the weather was all that could be eesired. Cyclists pursued their pastime with zest, and the leafy lanes of Cheshire were literally alive with wheelers. The facilities afforded by the railway companies for visiting popular resorts were largely taken advantage of, as the returns from the booking offiees show. As usual many people made the journey to Frodsham, where they enjoyed the invigorating breeze on the hills. Three hundred and sixty-four excursionists were booked to this village during the week-end, whilst 250 went to Chester, 130 to Llangollen and North Wales, 100 to Blackpool, and 100 to Birming- ham. On the Cheshire Lines railway 1,400 persons travelled to Liverpool, 500 to New Brighton, nearly 1,000 to Manchester, and 500 to Southport.

A pathetic case of suicide was inquired into at the Police Station on Tuesday evening by Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner. On Sunday morning an iron- worker named Solomon Brooks, 59 years of age, residing at 35, Kerfoot-street, took away his life by hanging himself in the scullery of his residence. He retired to bed as usual on Saturday evening and at seven o'clock the following morning his wife missed him. She did not suspect that there was anything wrong and went to sleep again. She got up about eight o'clock and on going into the scullery found deceased hanging by a rope attached to a hook in the ceiling. She sent for P.C. Lewis who lifted deceased from the hook andsaidl he was dead. It appeared that in January descea sed was discharged by his employers on account of old age and since that time his eyesight had been very bad. In consequence he had been very low-spirited and de- pressed, but his wife had never heard him threaten to take away his life.—The Deputy-Coroner said that no doubt deceased's mind had been unhinged through being out of work. So far as one could seg, the liability to be discharged on account of old age would not decrease in the future, but would be very much increased.—A verdict of "Suicide whilst of unsound mind" was returned.

div.head: Friendly Societys Conference.— Local Delegates.
div.p: Friendly Societys Conference.— Local Dele- gates.

Whit-week is now a recognized time for the holding of conferences by the friendly societies. During he past week the Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds halve met at Chorley ; the annual delegation of the order of Druids has beenlheld at Hull and the Oddfellows have held their annual conference at Cheltenham. At the last named conference several colonial delegates were welcomed. The board of directors in their report urged lodges and districts to make special efforts to reduce losses through secession. The actuary spoke of risks to the society by having members who were miners, and said that if these were to receive the bene- fits set forth in the rules their contributions would have to be doubled. It was stated that the bill before the House of Commons to penalise medical men for unprofessional conduct was aimed partly at doctors undertaking friendly society work, and in consequence it would be strongly opposed. The Warrington district of Oddfellows (Manchester Unity) has not been represented at the conference this year. Mr. Lawrence Weir and Mr. James Parr are the dele- gates representing the Warrington district at the annual conference of the Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds.

St. Ann's Choral Society. 1 About eleven weeks ago a choral society was formed in connection with St. Ann's Church and the project I was entered into so heartily that there is now a membership of thirty-six. Rapid progress has been made and on Tuesday evening the first public per- formance was given in the schoolroom,Dannett-street, before a fairly large audience. The Vicar (Rev. James Davies) occupied the chair. An admirable rendering of a service of song entitled "The two ' harvests was given and was greatly appreciated by the audience. Mr. W. Looker (deputy organist) conducted and Miss I Hewitt supplied the piano- ' forte accompaniments. The soles Were given i with good effect by the Misses Rigbey, Hard- man, and Travis, and Mr. W. Nunnerley, Mr. F. Taylor reading the connective passages. After the service of song an enjoyable ,miscellaneous pro- gramme of glees, anthems, and solos was submitted I and all the items were well received. Miss Hewitt ! sang "Flight of ages" and "Allan water" very I sweetly, and Mrs. Thomas was heard to advantage in " The village blacksmith." ,Mr. Bald rendered "My mother's Bible" in creditable style. A hearty vote ' of:thanks was accorded to the conductor, accompanist, and members of the• Society, the Vicar alluding in complimentary terms to the progress which had been made by the Society in so short a period.

LOOKING at England "LITTLE ENGLAND." from the illimitable

veldt, Mr.CHAMBER- LAIN has disoerned its littleness. What are its domestic politics? They are mere affairs of the parish pump. A new and determined struggle has begun against clericalism and a clerically- minded Government. How absurd! Why bother oneself to protest against legislation intended to turn little Nonconformists into little Churchmen when it would no so much easier to sit down and contemplate the vastness of the Empire? Greater statesmen than Mr. CHAMBERLAIN have been proud of little England. The Colonial Secretary is probably the first politician of rank who has gone so far as to profess that the dornestic'politics of his countrymen are beneath his notice. It is on the happiness and the prosperity and the content- ment of the people at home that the grestness of the Empire depends. It is little England that pays. But Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is like certain persons mentioned in the Scriptures, "whose eyes are in the ends of the earth." Having seen South Africa, he insists on regarding it as if it overwhelmed all ther interests. It seernq preposterous to inm, or he makes believe that it seems preposterous, that Englishmen should be concerned about their own affairs, that they should hold Hyde Park meetings, and object to pay a new Church rate, and care for the popular control of the schools, and think it worth while to preserve that system of free ex— change which has given us the lead alike in the commercial and industrial world. But when Mr. CHAMBERLAIN comes forward with the broad sug- gestion that we shall cut ourselves off from three-fourths of our trade in order that we may deal exclusively with our Colonies, which are responsible for only one-fourth, it becomes time to ask whether little England is not being treated rather too contemptuously by this megalomaniac statesman. Are we not entitled to fuller explana- tions? The country is really asked to surrender its independence in favour of the Colonies because it is Sc) little, though it is really as big as it has ever been. What specific proposal is there, what defined plan? None whatever. The plan is to be produced ;Olen the country has again reposed blind confidence in a Government which has twice deceived it in order to gain GE neral Elections, and has then used the power thus acquired for pur- poses wholly alien to those which were contem- plated by the people. What is suggested as matter to think over and vote upon when the time comes is the advisability of closing the door to the foreigner by means of high tariffs. We should then take all that we require from " our kin beyond the sea," axe:tiding our American kin, of course. The taxes levied on foreign goods would be earmarked for the purpose of paying old-age pensions. This supremely ridiculous proposal is exposed to contempt immediately it is stated in plain terms. Let us invert the order of the ideas underlying it. Old-age pensions are to be provided by taxation on imports; but we are not to tax imports from the Colonies, so that there can be no revenue from that source. The object of high tariffs, according to the suggested scheme, is to exclude.the goods of the foreigner, the Colonies, it is quite falsely said, being able to produce all that we require. But if we exclude the goods of the foreigner we cannot tax them, so that, obviously, there ean be no old-age pensions from this SCAMS. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S Scheme destroys itself. It is about as respectable and as businesslike as the prospectus of a bogus company promoter. The sacrifice that the English people are expected to make is enormous. The price of everything that we can consume would rise by just the amount ot the tariff and the cost of the collection, whether the goods purchased came from the Colonies or from our present foreign customers. Every country in Europe and in the New World would raise its tariff barriers against us. There would be no outlet for our trade and manufactures except to the Colonies, and the Object of Colonial Protection is to enable the Colonies to manufacture for themselves. From whatever point of view Mr. CHAMBSULAIN'S vaguely adumbrated scheme is considered it is equally impracticable and shoddy. But. as it ie.

merely required for electioneering purposes that does not greatly matter, perhaps. What is of real importance for the m nnent is the feeling it is Producing abroad. Ic is exasperating Europe, and especially Garmany. It is a challenge and a threat. If we wanted another war this might be good policy; but our greatest national need at Present is peace, and it is peace that Mr. CHAMBER- IN's schemes and manner of speech seem nicely calculated to endanger.

"Bank Holidays," HAPPY HOLIDAYS, said the BisuoP of AND OTHERS. STEPNEY the other day, "are killing the Possibility of happy holidays for the people." This must have been a hard saying for Lord -A.veimitY, who, even during his lifetime, is softie- times spoken of as "Se. LUBBOCK." On B tnk holidays all the people make holiday together. Dr. LANG, Bishop of Stepney, may consider this to be productive of evil, and perhaps to be an evil in itself. The ideal "happy holiday may be sup- posed to be represented by a family party, or .4 party of friends, not by a noun of multitude. Crowds engaged in the business of enjoyment are 'apt to become boisterous,and occasionally even riot- ous. The men drink too much,because they are jovial When they are in each other's company, and the Women encourage each other into excesses of bravura. Some such considerations as these may have been present in the BISHOP OF STEPNEY'S mind. He knows that sad East End of London Which is the centre of so many difficult problems, and B ink H )lidays in that region are apt to pre- out many revolting features. But we should be tclined to question whether holi lays anywher and everywhere, are not now much more seemly .than they were when they were much more infrequent. This view of the case is cer- tainly supported by the newspaper reports. In Cmost every town in England the plize are now much more severely:repressive of drunkenness And disorder than they were even a few years back; and yet there is in most places a steady diminution in the number of "Bank Holiday charges." This surely means :that the people are learning to use their holidays wisely—that they are making "happy holidays" of them, as Dr. LANG would have it. if that were not the case— if the BISHOP of STEPNEY'S declaration were really sound—the increase of holidays would be a national misfortune, whereas it appears to most of is that it has given more brightness to life and increased the true pleasures of living. The influence of holidays on the character of a People is a subject of no inconsiderable import- ance. It is not to be threshed out in a debating sOCiety, b.s Mr. BALFOUR says of Free Trade. Too Much holiday-making, there can be no doubt, lessens the sense of responsibility, develops light- ness of character, and makes industry irksome; but cur English holidays are neither numerous Inlough nor long enough to be open to condemna- tion on these grounds. Tney are still events of infrequent occurrence; but since the Bank holi- days have been added to those which were formerly customary they have, surely, done something to systematise the lives of the Industrious poor. It was not unusual for the Workmen in many industries to make a Bank eliclay of their own every Monday. The custom 1: Still observed in some trades and in particular 4,l4tricts, but is much more honoured in the breach _ 11"4411 the observance. "St. Lubbock" has a far better right to 7i place in the calendar than " St. Monday." To get a good holiday a little money roust be gradually saved, and therefore there must be less week-end waste. The habit of thrift is encouraged thus, though, it is true, the Whole of the savings will probably disappear at once, 'n one or two days of rernemberable enjoy- Ment. Those again, who look forward to the holi- days, and save up for them, will take pride in their dress and their appearance. They desire to "look well" when they go for a trip to the seaside or the Country. We are thus becoming, even as regards the poor, a people more carefully and expensively dressed. The children get something new to wear at the holiday seasons —new boots or a bonnet at Easter, a new suit or a frock at Whitsuntide; ands Se are young lives brightened, and white day Marked down in young memories. The tisuop of STEPNEY would, in all likeli- hood, have at once abandoned the idea that the possibility of happy holidays is being killed if he could have taken a fight on the Magicians carpet during the three or four days that have just passed:4way, and have looked down Over the edge at the happiness which was being enjoyed by the people in country and in town. Doubtless he would have seen much that is revolt- 'hg. There are still many thousands of those With whom holidlys are orgies ; but in general, we -take it, the tendency is towards the quieter forms of enjoyment and a more gentle behaviour. There IS also, as most employers would confess, more °Mena in the reture to work, and less disposition than there was to supplement the legal holiday by nne that may be said to be stolen.

We are able this week to give a glimpse of War- lington as it appeared to the compiler of a dictionary of the United Ki ngdom at the beginning of the Nineteenth Century. The Warrington of hundred years ago must indeed have looked very different from the Warrington of to-day. We are now able to count ourselves among the ig County Boroughs of the Kingdom, b the chro- racier of one hundred years ago had simply to atate that Warrington was a parish in the hundred tf West Derby, eleven miles from Nurthwich." *4 tiSt fancy, " Warrington, near Northwich "as an address. But it is when one comes to contrast the population that one recognises the lemarkable growth of the town. L.-ss than one undred years ago the population is stated to have ,u,oen 10,567;at the last census it was 64,241,50 that l'fle increase in the course of a century has been Then the females outnumbered the ?liaise, but as the last census revealed, the males 1° Warrington now outnumber the females. Local 4oglere will doubtless read with a sigh the remark 105 t the river at Warrinf,,rton " produces excel- elat fish !" What a change a single century brings about To think that the inky waters of the IViersey at Warrington once yielded fish to the herman's hook seems an impossible dream, but 740 can tell what the next century may reveal in ard to the purification of streams? It isquite within the range of possibility that some future onicler may be able to state that "the Mersey r°doces excellent fish," but we are afraid it will 'lot be in our time.

"Mr- F. Monks has, we are pleased to say,wiceded I°. very widely-expressed wish, and withdrawn t,-18 resignation of the Chairmanship of the Educe- -11 COMmittee. Thip decision was come to on -N,edhesday last week at a meeting between Mr. 'c'c'eks and most of the co-opted members of the 2rernittee, and will, there is no doubt,be a source 'rilr gratification to all who are directly concerned or interested in local educational affairs. There awill be more confidence in the committee with -1111°1, a man as Mr. Monks at the 73au of affairs, and just now a greater "measure of that confidence is urgently required.

The committee has some very serious and onerous work before it, for not only have the requirements of the new Act to be met, but, now that education is controlled by a central authority it devolves entirely upon that authority to make up Warrington's leeway in matters educational. How great that leeway is, only competent authorities an judge, but there is no question that the Act of last year has found Warrington very far behind the tinaes. While we recognise the need for economy in War- rington,we must emphasize what is almost a truism: that there can be no true economy on educa- tion. So far we have not observed any tendency on the part of the Education Committee to ex- travagance, though the proposal submitted at the last meeting involved so considerable an increase in standing expenses as to greatly alarm a large number of people who were not fully acquainted with the facts and who did not realise the extent of the task the committee has before it. The proposal to increase the salary of the Director by £lOO per year, was, aS all know, negativei, and an annual increase of 25 passed instead. This is equivalent to offering Mr. Murray £25 a year for the super- intendance of elementary education in 21 schools containing 13,596 scholars—not very princely pay! It is necessary for the welfare of the rising genera- tion that the city fathers of to-day should realise that the Education Committee must, to some ex- tent, be given a free hand. They alone can fully appreciate the needs of the occasion and in meet- ina those needs it is obvious that there will have to be considerable expenditure at the outset or Warrington will always be behind-hand in facili- ties for the education of its children.

Despite the many appeals for various charitable institutions to which the Warrington public are being asked to respond, it is gratifying to leirn that the Lifeboat institution is not to be forgotten. About five years ago Mrs. James Fairclough, who was then the Mayoress of the Borough, took a leading part in arranging for a collection on behalf of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution. The committee were enabled to forward a handsome donation to the funds of the institution, and there is still a balance in hand of something like £4O. This sum will form the nucleus of a more ambitious effort which is to be made in Warrington on behalf of the funds of the society on September sth. Dwellers in inland towns have not the same opportunity of estimating the worth of the Lifeboat Institution as those who ,live on the coasts of this " sea-girt isle," but there are few who are not aware of the humane and valu- able work of the Lifeboat Institution round our coasts in times of tempest and storm. Five years ago the public of Warrington showed their appre- ciation of this noble work and we have no doubt that they will make September 51.. h a record Life- boat Saturday for Warrington.

Trade is had, rates and rents are going up, and now the working man is to be deprived of his penny shave. There is probably nothing he would miss more—except his glass of beer, which we have often been told some proposal or other was going to rob him cf, particularly at election times. May-be the future has in store for us election cries of "Vote for so-and-so and a penny shave." Anyhow, the horny-handed, stubbly-chinned son of toil will be badly hit by the edict of the Warrington and District Hairdressers' Association which raises the price of shaving to lid. A rise of 50 per cent. is no trifle, and it may mean that the man who has hitherto luxuriously indulged in at least three shaves per week will in future content himself with only two, at the same expenditure. This is not :what our friends the barbers hope, however. Their case is also deserving of consideration. They had to do :some real hard work for a peon/ when customers of the blue-chinned stage-villain type came in- and they will only be moderately remunerated now that the price has gone up. But on the cal- low youths who enter the hairdressers with a feeling of manly pride they should reap a huge profit—something like a fraction of a farthing per hair. On the whole, judging fairly between the barber and his patrons, we think our sympathies are really with the former. He has to put in long hours, burn gas, and take a great many threehalF- pences, twopences, and fourpences before he can make ends meet, and after all, a minimum of 1-.ld per shave is hardly barefaced robbery, is it ?

We are glad of the assuranoe that no fever infected blankets have reached Warrington. At any rate the health authorities have been unable- to trace any notwithstanding a rigid search. It appears that a small consignment was sent to a tannery outside Warrington but the blankets were found to be unsuitable for the purpose for which it was intended to put them and they were all re- turned with the exception of one which has found its way into the possession of the village constable. Medical Officers of Health scattered all over the country have had the task imposed upon them of tracing infected blankets, which the War Office foolishly allowed enterprising middlemen to distribute second-hand at profitable rates. The question as to who will ultimately be held responsible for com- pensation in the case of blankets destroyed by the sanitary authorities is an interesting one. A large number of blankets have been destroyed by the Medical Officers' orders in various parts of the country, and the enormity of the offence commit- ted by the War Office can perhaps be effectually brought home to that inept Government depart- ment if it is called upon to pay compensation for all the blankets destroyed.

Tenants beware! We understand that a num- ber of property owners have already raised the rents of their tenants by 2d. or 3d. per week to recoup themselves for the additional expenditure entailed by the new Education rate. They are fully entitled to raise their rents, but not by 2d. and 3d, and this is the point we would have tenants to bear in mind. One penny per week advance on a 4s. 61. or is. house is sufficient to 'cover the extra rate for education, and in those cases where the landlord has put on 2d. or 3d. with this excuse he is obtaining more than he is entitled to and doing the tenants an injustice. We regret very much to find that there are War- rington landlords who are so ready and willing to seize the opportunity of raising rents, with both hands. It is easy to blame the Education Act, which, poor thing,has enough troubles of its own to bear, without unnecessarily incurring the wrath of the small householder who finds himself mulcted in an extra 3d. per week "for Educa- tion." On the other side of the case we have been equally pleased to learn that there are landlords with so much public spirit that they have not advanced the rents of their tenants by even one farthieg. They have voluntarily accepted an additional financial respriiibility for the education of their tenants' children, and, all honour to them! They could, with reason and fairness, have asked for another penny, but one penny only.

A new explanation of certain shortcomings by our manufacturers, which are made much of of pessimistic critics of our trade position,iF. tendered in an article in " Page's Magazine." If Britain has been obliged to import locomotives from America, and if the privilege of supplying British de• pendencies has been to sorno extent wrested from the hands of British manufacturers, it is, according to the writer, because of the overwhelm- ing success of the latter. British methods are not hopelessly obsolete, nor has tne star or British ascendency in this important branch of industry set for ever. Oa the contrary, says Mr. C. R iis- Martin, it has been a pronounced case of mbar). as de richesses ,all leading British maaufacturers being so utterly full up •of profitable work I that they have been absolutely unable to take any more for two years or so to come. We only wish the returns of employment in tho iron and steel industry bore out this optimiqtic statement. They hardly indicate a state of things in which plant is being worked at full pressare, and in which the chief anxiety of the principals is to find some reasonable ex also for recusiag the orders pouring upon them from all parts of the i world. div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
BEGGING.
At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, held on Tuesday, Sarah Moore,no fixed abode, was sent to Knutsford gaol for fourteen days for begginglon the evidence of P.C. Davies.

TRESPASSING ON SIR R. BROOKE'S ESTATE. At thd Runcorn Police Court on Friday, before Messrs. A. R. Norman, (in the chair) and J. Pritchard, a Liverpool man named James Bevan was charged with being drunk in Mersey-street, the day previous.—Pri- soner was further charged with destroying fern roots the property of Sir R. Brooke.—Prisoner pleaded guilty the evidence showing that he had only just come out of Warrington Hospital, but was a confirmed tramp. The damage done by the prisoner was considerable as he had disturbed the game in the woods in his two hours ramble through then..—Prisoner was also very violent in his cell.—Fined 7s. and costs for being drunk and 10s. and costs for the other offence, the Chairman stating that they were determined to put down such tres- passing.

div.head: TII E TRANSPORTER-SERIOUS ACC I DENT.
div.p: TII E TRANSPORTER-SERIOUS ACC I DENT.

On Wednesday an accident which might have been attended with very serious] results took 'place on the Widnes and Runcorn Transporter Company's works at Widnes. What is technically known as a stallage. 140 feet high, has been put up, and the crane has a 60 feet, jib. Shortly before 3 o'clock in the afternoon a sec- tion of one of the towers, weighing about 4 tons, was being hoisted into position, when something in connec- tion with the jib gaveway, and the iron work fell to the river. The jib broke in two, and also fell. A number of men were working at the time, and many of them had very narrow escapes. Fortunately, however, no one was injured. The stallage, on which were two men, rocked considerably, but kept in position.

div.head: WHITSUNTIDE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: WHITSUNTIDE AT RUNCORN.

Whitsuntide being regarded as Runcorn's greatest, holiday, work at the docks and chemical yards was entirely suspended until Wednesday morning. It has been the custom for many years for the Oddfellows, and friendly societies to parade the town on Whit- Monday morning, but for some reason this old-time custom was abandoned. In the afternoon the annual demonstration of Sunday schools was held, and was witnessed by a large number of people. The Church of England schools comprising the Parish Church, St. Michael's, Holy Trinity, and the Mersey Mission, formed :in procession and marched to the Vicarage, where they were joined by the children from the Weston School. After parading the town the scholars adjourned to the various schools, where they were entertained to tea. The Nonconformist schools held a similar demonstration, and marched to a field belonging to Mr. Sweetman, where games, &c., were participated in. Altogether there would be about 5,000 children in both processions.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT].

The Rev. J. Osborne, M.A., pastor of the Bethesda Congregational Church, has ha,da call to higher work. On Sunday last he announced at the evening service that he had tendered his resignation to the Church secretary and would leave in a few months. It is to be regretbed for many reasons that such an intellectual man as Mr. Osborne is leaving the town, where for some half dozen years he has laboured so eaenestly. We can ill spare gentlemen with such distinctions. Run- corn will certainly be intellectually the poorer whenhe enters his new sphere of labour.

At the Council meeting yesterday (Thursday) a very important and honourablc, appointment had to be made —no less than that of the appointment of a representa- tive on the Committee of the Liverpool University. The Technical Instruction Committee very wisely chose Mr. F. J. Norman,and one Would have thought the name would havc, been confirmed by the Council without demur. But Mr. Wiswall, in anarrow parochial spirit contended that the Council alone 'contained the embodi- ment of wisdom and knowledge, and that, therefore, the Council were not justified in selecting as the representa- tive an outsider. Happily, this restricted view did not meet with the approval of the Council, and Mr. Wiswall's amendment was defeated. Mr. Norman is to be con- gratulated on his being recognised as the "fit and proper man" for such an appointment.

It is to be regretted that the Runcorn and Widnes transporter will be retarded by the extremely unfor- tunate accident which occurred on NVednesday. The crane, which has a 60 feet jib, and which is erected on a stallage 140 feet high, is used to get the iron .work in position, and under the strain of lifting a tower, in weight four tons, suddenly gave way. There were several narrow escapes. It is stated that the accident will delay the erection of the bridge considerably.
