div.head: Examiner Friday, June 5, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner Friday, June 5, 1903.

ground when he asserts that British competitors have had contracts wrested from them by unfair means. It is notorious that in certain cases impossible tenders have been made by foreign contractors, and an attempt made to pass off in- ferior work. Honesty, however, is, in the long run, the best policy, even in the execmion of con- tracts.

Mr. Seddon's proposal to establish, on behalf of the New Zealand Government, butchers' shops in Great Britain marks another step in Imperialism. The tradesmen at home will complain, and there is no doubt that this interference in their business by a trust that can undersell them with profit is a serious menace. But the honest have to suffer for the unscrupulous. If there had not been such an extensive sale of Canterlaury mutton as English-fed stock the colonists would not, even at che instance of Mr. Seddon, have been stirred on to this enterprise. Tin quantity of foreign mutton imported into this country has increased by 50 per cent. in the last five years, although inquiry in the kitchens would not lead to any such discovery of fact. The New Zealander naturally desires to get the benefit of his grazing, and to ensure a perm Anent trade, free from the caprice of the middleman. The statement that the Government will sell at a price simply "to cov3r cost" must not be taken too exactly. What it means is that the Government will not want a profit on its own account; bat it will take care that the farmer has a go )d one. This bond of trade, secured without any interference with our fiscal policy, will commend itself to most persons outside the assailed class. When Ministers enter upon such enterprises, however, the quiet men who are afraid to allow a Corpora- tion to mend a water-tap lest it should be called municipal trading receive a shock. They must feel that with the new century is beginning a new era in commercial systems. It may be good or bad; but we cannot stand still.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
The fortnightly meeting of the above Board was held on Tuesday under the presidency of Mr. J. Stokes.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT APPROVAL,
A letter was received from the Local Government Board sanctioning payment to the Clerk, Mr. G. F. Ashton, of £lOO for his services to the Union Assess- ment Committee.

div.head: GRANT.
div.p: A GRANT.

Mr. W. E. Knollys, assistant secretary to the Local Government Board, wrote respecting a report made by the Inspector, Mr. Dansey, re Eliza Hayes, industrial teacher at the Workhouse, and certifying that the sum due to the Guardians under the Local Government Actwould include a payment of £l6 3s. 4d. per annum, in respecti of the salary of that officer for the year end- ing Marsh 25th 1904.

div.head: AN APPLICATION.
div.p: AN APPLICATION.

A letter was received from Edith Cunnah, assistant matron, asking for an increase of salary. She was at present receiving £2O, subject to £1 4s. deduction. Mr. Guest gave notice of motion that at the next meeting an increase of salary should be allowed, and a similar course was pursued respecting the application of the nurse, who asked for a clear £3O yearly. •

div.head: PRESENTATION OF A MEDAL.
div.p: PRESENTATION OF A MEDAL.

A letter was read from Miss M. N. Kett stating that Nurse Hampshire had been awarded a silver medal by the Northern Workhouse Nursing Association on the completion of her three years work and asking the Board to present it to her. On the motion of Mr. Mosely-Williams who said that Nurse Hampshire had always done her work satisfac- torily it was resolved that the Clerk despatch the medal to her with a suitable letter.

VAC C INATION. IVIr. 'E. Docker, clerk to the King's Norton Union enclosed the following resolution passed at the last meeting of his Board :—"That it is desirable that the Vaccination Act should not be administered by Boards of Guardians, but should be undertaken by the local Sanitary Authority." The co-operation of other Boards was solicited with the matter ancl the -views made known.

A memorial was also read from the Wigan Union to the Local Government Board, the Wigan Union express- ing the hope that the Runcorn Board would adopt the same attitude. The memorial set forth the enormous increase in the fees paid to public vaccinators since the passing of the Education Act, 1898, which could be reduced without hardship to such officers and still adequately prevent the spread of small-pox. The petitioners recommended a payment of 2s. 6d in respect of ever successful vaccination at the home of the person vaccinated, and is. 6d. if performed at the public vaccinator's surgery. Both communications were referred to the Parlia- mentary Co mmittee.

div.head: RUNCORN URBAN COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN URBAN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the above Council was held on Thursday morning in the Council Chamber under the presidency of Mr. R. IL Posnett. Present—Messrs. D. Bisbrown, J. H. Salkeld, W. Handley, F. %%wall. E. Gatley, E. liaison, S. Walton, G. Hewitt, G. Jones,with Messrs. F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), J. Wilding (surveyor), and Dr. McDougall (medical officer).

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.
div.p: THE MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.
Dr. McDougall reported that the deaths for the past monthnumbured 17 and the births 52. PURCHASE OF THE KING'S PORTRAIT.

The Highways and Buildings Committee recommen- ded that a mezzo-tint engraving of His Majesty King Edward VII. from the original portrait by Mr. Luke Fildes' R.A. be purchased, and that it be placed in the Council Chamber.

div.head: TILE FIRE BRIBADE.
div.p: TILE FIRE BRIBADE.

The Markets and Cemetery Committee recommended that the offer of the Ocean Accident and Guarantee Corporation to issue a policy of insurance against acci- dents to the members of the Runcorn Fire Brigade at a premium of 3s. 6d. per man be accepted. (MOO at death or permanent total disablement, £5O for permanent par- tial disablement, also weekly compensation for tem- porary disablement) ; that the Fire Brigade be supplied with the following articles : Six lengths of canvas hose with instantaneous couplings, ten life lines, two swan neck branches with 2 inch jets, six leather hose clips, one jumping sheet and two ladder (hose) clips. Approved on the motion of Messrs. Walton and Hewitt.

div.head: LIVERPOOL ErNIVERSITY COURT.
div.p: LIVERPOOL ErNIVERSITY COURT.

The Technical Instruction Committee recommended that F. J. Norman, Esq.? J.P., be appointed a member of the Court of the Liverpool University for three years as from Ist January, 1903. Mr. Handley moved the adoption of the minutes stating that it was very pleasing to think that Runcorn on account of its work for secondary education had been honoured by being asked to appoint a representa- tive. Wallasey, with a population of 56,000, was the only Urban Council besides Runcorn which had been similarly asked. Mr. Thsbrown seconded, eulogising Mr. Normanas a fit and proper man for such a position. Mr. Wisvvall opposed the motion and moved that a member of the Council be appointed. It was not fair for the Council to do all the donkey work and other men to carry off the honourable positions. They should appoint a member of the Council who could report his work on the Liverpool Committee. _

Mr. Jones seconded the amendment, Sir. Tmison stating that he could not follow Mr. Wiswall's lead though he recognised that there was something to be said in his view of the case. The amendment was lost and the minute was confirmed.

div.head: EDUCATION ACT.
div.p: THE EDUCATION ACT.

A letter was read from the Cheshire County Council inviting the Urban Council to submit the names of more than one person eligible for appointment by the County Council as its representative manager of the Voluntary Schools within the Urban District of Runcorn. It was resolved that the names of Messrs. E. Imison and A. R. Norman be sent to the County Council.

div.head: TPIE LOCAL EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: TPIE LOCAL EDUCATION COMMITTEE.

After some discussion it was resolved that in reply to the County Council Messrs. Wilson,Handley, Jones, and Pritchard be appointed as the Urban Council's repre- sentatives on the Local Education Committee.

div.head: CHESHIRE CHAMBER OF AGRICULTURE. Sir John Brunner and the Farmers.
div.p: CHESHIRE CHAMBER OF AGRICULTURE. Sir John Brunner and the Farmers.

A meeting of the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture I took place atCrewe on Monday, Mr. R. Tollemache, M.P., presiding. The secretary said that at its last meeting the chamber passed a resolution asking Parlia- ment, in view of the serious •increase in local rates re- sulting from parish and district and country councils' administration and by the inclusion of large and grow- ing urban and semi-urban districts with rural parishes, to make the Agricultural Rates Act permanent. In acknowledging that resolution, Sir John .Brunner. Bart., M.P., wrote—` I desire to point out that the large and growing urban districts which the chamber looks upon with disfavour are one and all peopled with customers of yours, who, being near at hand, are for that reason more valuable customers than the inhabitants of distant cities. Perhaps I ought to say that lam well aware that huge quantities of agri- cultural produce are sent into the cities to come back by rail to these urban districts and that farmers thereby lose much of the advantage of having customers near by ; but I submit to you that there is, or might be, a large and distinct set-off from your point of view against any disadvantage to farmers in the neighbour- hood of these gr,owinf, districts. I might add that works like Brunner; Mond and Co.'s pay enormous con- tributions, which are a pure net gain to the farmers. We do not use the roads, we provide our own water, our own sewers, our own lighting, and the number of people relieved out of the poor rate is no more to-day than it was when we Started employing 60 men, thirty years ago. During those years I have seen land near to us . grow in value from 28s. an acre to £6O per acre. and that land pays only half rates under the Agricultural Rates Act. No one can expect me to agree in making such au Act permanent." Mr. J. limberton said that Sir John Brunner Itiaditus- construed the resolution of the chamber. The chamber did not look with disfavour upon urban districts, but were anxious to work harmoniously with them. What the chamber asked for was that the burden of taxation should be properly apportioned. Mr. R. Morris (Chester) said that farmers had to pay their proportion of large costs for the provision of i water, sewers lighting, &c., from which they did not de- rive any benefit. ' Mr. Millington (Northwich) said that in the district of Lostock a water, sewage, and lighting scheme was introduced, and farmors living three miles away had to ! contribute to the cost, although they got not the smallest benefit from it.

After further discussion, a resolution was passed that the secretary of the chamber should send a letter to Sir ;John Brunner, pointing out that farmers, "threatened, as they are, with continual extensions of rating for matters that offer little or no direct benefit to them as occupiers of land, feel themselves justified in asking that the long-promised alteration in the basis of rating shall be made, that will equitably apportion those charges according to the benefits resulting to the various classes of property." A letter was read from the clerk of the county coun- cil, stating that with the view of preventing the spread of anthrax the council had authorised the chief constable to purchase a cremator for the destruction of animals found infected with the disease.—A resolution was passed, asking Parliament to introduce a Bill making railway companies responsible for damage to crops, plantations, caubeti by sparks from passing locomotives.—A letter was read from the. War Office, in reply to a resolution asking that purchasers of remounts for the army should attend the camps of yeomanry while they are in training, stating that" if , the convenience of the public service admits, an I officer will be sent."

EARLESTOWN_ MAY QUEEN
FESTIVAL

Beautiful weather favoured the festival of crowning the" Queen of May" at Earlestown on Saturdayafter- noon. The early morning was distinctly unfavourable, and there were many anxious glances heavenwards. A 4 noon approached, however, the threatening clouds were dispelled, and the sun broke forth in all its glory, and the remainder of the day was oright and genial. 'Visi- tors from the neighbouring towns and villages poured in by train, waggonette and bicycle, and soon locomo- tion became difficult, especially about the Market place and its approaches. From noon until about two o'clock, characters of all descriptions could be seen wending their way to the Market Ground, which had been enclosed with canvas, completely shutting out all except those taking part in the festival. The streets also, from a decorative point of view, bore a pretty appearance, the tradespeople having with the private residents, decorated their pre- mises with banners and streamers. As the various characters mustered on the place of rendezvous, the marshals, Messrs. Duncan, Jones, Dean, Boardman, Clough, Clayton, and Dr. Mouncey, busily employed themselves in arranging them in their proper sections, and in the order of procession,a task by no means light,. Prizes having been offered for light and heavy turn- outs, there was a good entry and a close competition. The adjudicator for the turnout class was Mr. J. Dodson, of Huyton,and there was no doubt that he hada difficult task before him to choose the best out of the heavy turnouts. Subsequently however the highest award was given to the Newton Urban District Council (J. Adam driver). The second prize went to Fairclough's (G. Ogden driver), Earlestown, and the third to the Vulcan Foundry Company, (S. Dodd,driver). A special prize was given by Mr. butts of a double martindale and breastplate, and the Sankey Sugar Works (Mr. J. Dutton, driver) was the successful competitor Tradesmen's turnouts numbered five and the following were the judge's awards: (1), E. Parkinson (J. Anders, driver), Earlestown; (2) Sharp (J. Ashcroft, driver), Earlestown; (4) The River Plate Meat Company, (S. Platford, driver), Earlestown. The special prize of a handbag given by Mr. Cutts, was won by Mr. Basker- ville, Bridge-street, Earlestown. During the judging of , the turnouts the procession was ready to wend • its way I along the line of route. The procession exceeded all expectations. The committee who had promoted the brilliant affair promised to surpass all previous festivals, land there was no doubt that their efforts were met with success. iThe honour attached to the position of the May Queen was conferredlupon Miss Louie Cartwright, who I in her Coronation robes looked exceedingly pretty. The I situation on her part was filled with dignity, and her trainers are to be congratulated on the way in which she tilled the details of royal deportment. Her robes were of white silk trimmed with pale cream lace and insertion let in. From the shoulders was a handsome train of crimson plush which was trimmed all round the border with ermine. Her crown was of white silk trimmed with crimson plush, and was ornamented with imitation gems and pearls. Her slippers were of white satin. She carried a charming bouquet of white and crimson flowers. Her lady-in-waiting (Miss L. Dale) was arrayed in cream silk with lace trimmings, itc, Masters Berty Ball and Percy Haynes were the pages in attendance and Masters Reggie Dale and Clarence Shallcross were the trainbearers. They were adorned in red plush and silver-plated buttons. The maids of honourfiwere Misses Worsley, Insley, Thune, Gerrard, Barton, A, and M. Downham, and Millard, and they were drawn in a carriage kindly lent by Mr. Haskins. Preceding the Royal carriage were the sword bearer (Master R. Bancroft), sceptre bearer (Master J. Jackson), and crown bearer (Master J. Lunwame). They were dressed in blue, purple and red plush , respectively. The Lord Chancellor (Master Cyril Kilminster) and the Clerk of the Courts (Master Harold Brown) also preceded the carriage in a convey- ance. On each side of the Queen's carriage was a naval body guard under the supervision of Instructor Barton, late of the 7th Dragoon Guards. This being the second occasion on which a May Queen festival has been held the ex-Queen (Miss L. Clayton) took part in the pro- cession. She was drawn in a carriage and pair, attended by her lady-in-waiting (Miss L. Ogden). The Queen was dressed in white silk with beautiful lace trimmings ' and wore her crown,and the lady-in-waiting was arrayed in a dress of similar design, whilst the maids of honour Misses N. Naylor and E. Faulkner, wore cream silk dresses with insertion. The train bearers were Masters F. Houghton and W. Pope. The tableaux were this year exceedingly pretty and in all seventeen competed for the three prizes offered for the best lurry. Mrs. , Gange, Mrs. Dowling and Mrs. Ainley were the judges and the following were their awards 1, "Little 80-Peep and Boy Blue," Miss D. Tiffin and Master J. Valentine; I 2, "Rock of Ages" Miss Naylor; 3, "United we stand— England, Ireland and Scotland " Miss L. Barrow, Miss Kilminster and Miss A. Owen.

The first prize winner was an exceedingly pretty turn- 1 out and stood out in prominence and effectiveness. The two figures were both dressed in pale blue, and standing near them were two little lambs. The limy was decor- , ated in cloth to match, and it was evident that no pains or expense had been spared to prepare the tableau for the occasion. The second successful lurry, "Rock of Ages" was exceedingly pretty. Miss Naylor, of Altrincham, who was the principle character ' was a pretty girl, with long tresses of luxuriant hair. This flowing down her beautiful white gown gas,* most faithful reproduction of that well- known picture. Sergeant and Mrs. Lings were respon- sible for the production, and deserve hearty congratula- tion for the time and expense they had taken to bring about a successful termination. "United we stand," representing Great Britain was oapitally por- trayed. The Floral Queen was another very pretty tableau, and was represented by Miss Gladys Daly who was accompanied by fous ladies-in-waiting. Another popular tableau was the White Slave, impersonated by Miss Powell. The . picture represented a white girl captured by brigands. She was tied to a tree and round a table was a group of her captors gambling. The Angels of Peace was another very prett,, tableau and was faithfully depicted by Misses E. Stoke, B. Arm- strong, E. Turner, E. Armstrong, and A. J. Elliot. The Violet Queen who was the first prize winner the previ- ous year, again called for much admiration, and the central figure, Miss Price, was arrayed in a most charm- ing dress of white and violet silk trimmed with bunches of violets. Her ladies in waiting were dressed in similar coloured dresses. The lurry was a mass of glow- ing colour and one of the most prominent in the pro- cession.

45 Over a thousand took part in the procession. The ; procession left the Market by way of Oxford-street,and proceeded! along Haydock-street,Cross-lane, Crow-lane West to the top of New-road, Market street,Legh-street, Viaduct-street, Kyle-street, Queen-street, King-street, Bridge-street, Market-street, Oxford-street to the ground. The whole of the route was lined with spec- tators, who now and again raised rounds of applause as the performances or characters appealed to them. The May Queen naturally commanded the most attention. At intervals the procession was brought to a standstill to allow the morris dancers to perform. When the gay pageant arrived at the ground a hearty cheer was given , for the Queen, who was escorted to the throne which was covered with a pretty canopy, and as she ascended the platform the Earlestown Band played a fitting selection of music. Britanniaafterwards took a seat on the right hand. The crowning of the Queen was wit- nessed with great admiration, and Mrs. F. Dowling,wife of Dr. Dowling of Earlestown in placing the crown upon the Queen's head. said "Louie Cartwright I crown you Queen of the May. I hope your Majesty will be happy and prosperous and that your subjects will remain loyal and faithful." The performance of the ceremony was greeted with loud applause and on the band striking up "God save the King," the people raised their hats. Subsequently the sceptre was placed in the Queen's arms, and the roll was signed. Afterwards a long and varied programme ; was gone through, including the Maypole dance by 28 , children, the Highland dance by 48 artistes in national costumes, entertainments by the Yah Yah Coons, veleta dance by 48 children with tambourines,cutlass:exercise by Naval Brigade and a special novelty, plaiting the May- pole by Highland dancers. After the whole programme ; had been gone through, dancing was indulged in until dusk. In the afternoon Mr. Oswalis Silverstone made the following awards for gentleman cyclists in char- acter:—(l) Mr. Jackson (Tyldesley) "The Handyman.' Lady cyclists in character: (.1) Miss Gertrude Mitchell ; (Golborne), •` The Nautch girl"; (2) Miss Martha Rose (Earlestown) - Pictorial Magazine." Comic cyclists , in costume: (1) Mr. S. div.head: Minor Cases. Warrington Borough Police Court.
div.p: Minor Cases. Warrington Borough Police Court.
FRlDAY.—Before Mr. H. Roberts (in the chair), Alder _ _ man Smethurst, Messrs. Thornton and Young. _

MISSED HIS OPPORTUNITY.—WiIIiant Reynoas, 34, Cartwright-street, was summoned for not having hadhis child vaccinated.—Mr. Holford, vaccination officer, proved the case and asked for an order for the child to be vaccinated within 14 days.—Defendant said he did not believe in vaccination, but the Chairman told him that he was bound to have the child vaccinated as he had neglected the opportunity to apply for an exemp- tion.—The order was granted. DOMESTIC TnousLEs.—James Dunn, a furnaceman residing at 67, Forshaw-street, was summoned for assaulting his wife, Sarah Ellen Dunn on May 20th.— Mr. Steel appeared for the complainant and Mr. Browne defended.—lt was alleged that defendant came home under the influence of drink and refused to have his tea. He wanted his wife to go out for drink but she would not and when she refused to give him money to obtain drink he thumped her inflicting marks on her arms and body. She went out and returned later but defendant would not admit her to the house until two o'clock in the morning.—Defendant stated that his wife picked pp a cup with the intention of throwihg it at him. He endeavoured to take it from her and in the struggle she banged her head against the cupboard door.—Defendant was fined 10s. and costs (21 2.5.) with the option of 14 days imprisonment. AssAuLT.—Mary Jarvis, 38, Forster-street, was sum- moned for assaulting Mary Cogan, 36, Forster-street, on May 21st—Complainant said defendant struok her in the face.—Defendant admitted the assault but said com- plainant first struck her.—A fine of ss. and costs was imposed. THREATS.—Jane Hardman, Erwood-street, was sum- moned for making use of threats towards Mary Ann Gannon, Erwood-street, on May 24th.—She was bound over to keep the peace and ordered to pay 10s. costs. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
GROSS NEGLECT OP GRILDREN-MOTHER GAOL.

A bad case of child neglect. was heard at the Warring- ton Police Court on!Friday, the defendant being Alice Concannon, wife of a Corporation foreman, residing at Raddon Cottage. She was charged with neglecting her four children in a manner likely to cause them un- necessary suffering and injury to health.—Mr. Crompton prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C., and said the Society %ere of opinion that the case ought to be tried at Quarter Sessions under the Inebriates Act. He had mentioned the matter to Mr. White who did not think the circumstances would quite justify the adoption of that course. Defendant's husband earned 265. per week and gave his wife 225. The sole cause of the neglect was drink. Defendant had been warned and I dealt with by the magistrates with a view to bringing about an improvement but she still persisted in neglect- lag the children. During the afternoon of May 20th Inspector Hackett and Mr. Taylor, P.C.M. visited the house and found defendant lying drunk onthe sofa with her five months old baby in her arms,and an empty beer bottle lying on:the top of her. The house and children were in a filthy condition and the rooms smelled horribly. Even on that day as soon as defendant came round a bit she sent for more drink. On May 22nd the Inspector again visited the house with Constable Hardy and matters were just as bad. Defendant had been seen in the streets in the pouring rain drunk with a child in her arms. He contended that this was a very gross case of neglect.—lnspector Hackett gave evidence as to the shocking condition of the house and children. Other witnesses were called and the Chief Constable said defendant was sentenced to a month's imprison- ment for a similar offence in June last. She was recently sent to goal for seven days for being drunk whilst in charge of a child.—Defendant, who asked for another chance, was sent to prison for a month. A WARRINGTON HUSBAND'S BRUTALITY. • At the County Borough Police Court, on Friday, Henry Clare, Flag-lane, was summoned for persistent cruelty to his wife, Mary Clare.—Mr. Steel appeared for the complainant, and Mr. Crompton defended.—Mr. Crompton admitted the cruelty, and consented to an order, but the magistrates required acts of cruelty to be specified.—Mr. Steel said that the acts of cruelty were most horrible and revolting, and one could hardly imagine that a man holding defendant's position would have been guilty of them. The parties hadbeen married for twenty years, and the first act of cruelty appeared to have been committed some three months after the marriage. Defendant had continually thrown plates, knives, pokers, basins, jugs, and anything he could lay his hands on at the plaintiff. He seemed to be a man of uncontrollable temper, and whenever any- thing went wrong in his work he came home and 'took his spite" out of his wife. About six months ago a stable boy in the employ of the defendant knocked down a wall with a cart and this seemed to have annoyed him very much. He went home and beat his son and whenhis wife remonstrated with him he pulled down the blinds and was about to thrash her when a friend named Brooks came in and prevented any assault. On the following day defendant thrashed the 'boy with a whip used for thrashing young horses. He afterwards pulled down the blinds, locked all the doors, and thrashed complainant unmercifully till blood ran down her face. On another occasion he overturned a bucket of dirty water on the floor, mixed it with sand, and thrashed his wife because she would not clean it up. Another day when he was annoyed because the stable boy had collided with gentleman's horse he overturnedthe table which was laid ready for dinner and broke the crockery. Helrepeated this conduct at tea time and *hilsthis wife was picking up the pots he seized her y the hair, pulled her round the kitchen, and struck her with his closed fist, inflicting a black eye. On another date he threw a basin at her inflicting a gash in her arm and she had to have six stitches nut in by Dr, Curtis. He had also kicked her and caused an abcess on her ankle. On the day whenshe left him he complained because her uncle had written a letter in reference to his conduct. e told her he was going to see thelcolour of her blood before she slept that night and that he would kill her and hit her when she was dead. He then went out telling her to be prepared when he returned but on the advice of her sister complainant left the house. Defendant earned 355. per week and paid a boy Us. He also received £4O or £5O per annum for breaking in horses and his shop made at least £3 per week profit. He was also paid for acting as liberator in connection with a homing society, and made about £7 a year for clipping horses. —Complainant asked for an order for at least 30s. per week.—Mr. Crompton stated that after paying the stable boy defendant's wages amounted to 255., which he gave to his wife. She also managed the shop and received the takings. The business was, however, insolvent. The other amounts mentioned by Mr. Steel were exaggerated Defendant wished the magistrates to give him the. custody of three of the ch ldren .After some discussion an order was granted with 30s.per week alimony,complainant to have the custody of the children. An advocate's fee was allowed. CONSTABLE AND CIVILIAN ASSAT.TLTED.—"LIKB A MAD

div.head: DOG."
div.p: DOG."

William Cotton, last fr:rniilackburn, appeared in the dock at the Warrington Police Court on Monday,on the charges of having been drunk and disorderly in Sankey- street on Saturday evening and assaulting Constable Cooper and James Barker.—P.C. Cooper said he was on duty near Trinity Church and saw the prisoner, who was very drunk, surrounded by a large crowd. He was shouting at the top of his voice that the magistrates and police were "a pack of thieves and rogues." Witness took him into custody and in Palmyra-square prisoner became very rough. He kicked witness about the legs and butted him in the stomach and a man named James Barker, who came to witness's assistance, also received kicks and was bitten on the fingers.—The Chief Constable said he saw the prisoner in Palmyra-square and he was biting and gnashing like a mad dog. The constable handled him 'exceedingly judiciously and mercifully.—James Barker, corroborated, the Chief Constable remarking that the witness assisted Cooper very pluckily and efficiently.— Prisoner, who had been before the Court 17 times and had often been to gaol,lwas sentenced to three months imprisonment with hard labour. The witness Barker, who had previously rendered similar assistance to the police, was awarded ss.
A VfOLE:s.iT TRAM PASSENGER.-SMART PENALTY AT
WARRINGTON.

A young man named Joseph Salt,residing at 2,Mi11-lane, appeared before Mr. F. Monks and other magistrates at the Warrington Police Court on Monday to answer to four charges viz., making use of obscene language on a tramcal travelling between Wilderspool and Bridge- street at 9.10 on Saturday night, assaulting Daniel i Barton, conductor, n f!ylands-street, assaulting Police Sergeant Smith, and wilfully breaking a pane of glass in the window of a cell at the Police Station on Sun- day afternoon, doing damage to the amount of 2s. 6d.— Prisoner pleaded not Fruity to all the charges except the last, stating that he broke the window because he wanted more air.— Daniel Barton, tram conductor, residing at 55, Cartwright_ street, stated that about nine o'clook on Saturday night a car was proceeding between Wilderspool and Rylanda street. He noticed the prisoner on the top of the car sitting on one seat with his feet resting on another. Witneas'requested him to take his feet off the seat and prisoner after at first demurring did so. Subsequently he resumed his original position and on again being spoken to he made use of obscene language. When the car arrived at Rylands street witness naked prisoner for , his name and address. He was writing the name dow I

div.head: SAVED BY HIS BIBLE.
div.p: SAVED BY HIS BIBLE.
Welshman's Strange Story.

An extraordinary story is that of Mr. David Jones, a Welsh tinplate worker. Mr. Jones has lived for a quarter of a centuryat Moniston, South Wales, where his present address is 38a Bush-road, Old Bridge. His life was without incident, but one day he suddenly com- menced to shudder, and the next moment fell down un- conscious. He was taken home, and found to be com- pletely paralysed. For weeks he lay in bed unable to speak or move, and for fifteen years he:suffered without hope. His savings became gradually exhausted, until at last he had no money to buy medicine. As a last resource, acting on the suggestion of a friend who brought him a ray of hope by telling him of his own cuie by Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people, he actually sold his most cherished possession—his Bible, and bought some boxes of these pills. "It was with the gravest misgivings and the most profound regret that I parted with the Book," he said, 'and gave up the joy of turning its loved pages. Happily its contents are stored in my mind, or I could not have borne the loss even for the hope of health, happily in the end fulfilled. "I felt great benefit soon after I commenced to take the pills' and before I had finished the first box I was able to take my meals more regularly and enjoy them. My strength gradually came back to me for the first time in fifteen yeacs. After taking four boxes I was so well that I was able to get about, and am now so well that I am able to work.'

Few more striking and pathetic stories are on record. Paralysis is one of the most frequent causes of total disability, and its dangers constantly threaten all active workers. Broken-down nerves, a weak back, loss of balance, and any sort of numbness in the members are early symptoms. Remember the awful disease which they threaten! Dr. Williams' Pink Pills are not merely a cure, but they can prevent the onset of disease. They should be taken in time. When they can cure the most hopeless cases—and this is abundantly proved—it is no wonder that minor ailments of life yield so much more readily to them than to any other medicine ever dis- covered. Nervous and spinal weakness, nenralgia,head- aches, and backaches, St. Vitus' Dance, are allied to paralysis. Dr. Williams' pink pills are noted for their good effects on Women. They are the greatest and safest general tonic medicine ever discovered. Dr. Williams' medicine company, Holborn-viaduct, London, supply the pills post free at two shillings and ninepence per box if any difficulty should be experienced in obtaining the genuine article. It is to be noted that substitutes are entirely unavailing, and that it was the genuine pills which cured Mr. David Jones, and enabled him to buy back his cherished Bible.

div.head: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
Smith—Bennett.

At Bold-street Wesleyan Church on Monday the marriage was solemnized of Mr. John D. Smith, son of, Mr. H. Smith, Lincoln, and Miss Martha Bennetts youngest daughter of Mr. Benjamin Bennett, Clapgate. Farm, Bewsey. The officiating minister was the Rev G. H. Carnson, Superintendent of the Circuit. The bride, who was given away by her father, was charm- ingly attired, and carried a bouquet of lilies and stephanotis. Her bridesmaids were Miss Mary Bennett (sister) and Miss Muriel Evans (cousin of the bride), whose bouquets were of pink carnations. The duties of best man wereclischarged by Mr. George Smith, brother of the bridegroom. The newly married couple who weretha recipients of numerous and costly presents de- parted during the day for Colwyn Bay where the honey moon is being spent.

Taylor—Smith A fairly-large congregation assembled in Wycliffe Congregational Church on Tuesday forenoon for the purpose of witnessing the marriage of Mr. Charles I Frederick Taylor, formerly of Warrington, but now of Newcastle-on-Tyne,and son of the late Mr. John Taylor, of this town, with Miss Mary Eleanor Smith, daughter of Mr. John Smith, of Lovely-lane. The bride, who was given away by her father, was becomingly attired in a dress of cream cloth and silk, with white chiffon hat to match. She carried an exquisite shower bouquet of roses and lilies of the valley. She was attended by her sister, Miss Beatrioe Hannah Smith, as brides- maid. She was attired in a dress of Bale blue voile trimmed with silk and lace, and wore 'a black picture hat. Her bouquet was composed of tea roses and forget- me-nots, the gift of the bridegroom, who also presented her with a gold neck-lace. The duties of best man were satisfactorily discharged by Mr. Henry Hayes. The Rev. John Yonge (pastor of the church) officiated and Mr. W. H. Payton, Mug. Bac., presided at the organ and played several appropriate voluntaries. The newly- married couple left the church to the strains ofMendels- sohn's familiar "Wedding March." A reception was afterwards held at the house of the bride's father, at which about 40 guests were present. early in the after- noon Mr. and Mrs. C. F. Taylor left for their new home at Heaton, Newnastle-on-Tyne. They were the recipi- ents of a large number of choice wedding presents.

div.head: WALKING MATCH AT PADGATE.
div.p: WALKING MATCH AT PADGATE.

Padgate has not escaped the walking mania. On Wednesday evening there was a walking match for prizes subscribed by the inhabitants generally. The route decided upon was about seven miles in length. Starting from the Stocks Inn Padgate, the competi- tors were to proceed via "The Noggin" at Culcheth, Croft, Crab-lane and back to the Stocks Inn. About a dozen competitors entered and at 7 30 p.m., Mr. George Mather, district Councillor started them on their journey. The judges were Messrs. Unwin, Haslam an Grounds. The first man to arrive at the winning post was Thomas Potter who reached the Stocks Inn at 8.40, having covered the distance of seven miles in one hourand ten minutes. He was closely followed by Joe Mather who secured the second prize. The third and fourth prizes were secured by James Potter and J. White respectively. div.head: "OAK TREE" INN, NEWTON. -- Unsuccessful Opposition to the Transfer of
div.p: THE "OAK TREE" INN, NEWTON. -- Unsuccessful Opposition to the Transfer of
the Licence.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednes- day, Mr. A. Browne, on behalf of James Henry Toft, asked the magistrates to authorise the clerk to give a certified copy of the licence of the" Oak Tree "urn Newton. He stated that the licence was granted at Newton on February 12th, and sinoe then the house had changed hands. During the removal the liceace had been lost and could not be discovered.
The application was granted. Mr. Browne then applied for the licence of the inn to be transferred from James Henry Toft to Herbert Butterworth.

Mr. 11. J. Longton said he opposed the application on behalf of the executor of the late Mrs. Gorse, who was formerly the licencee of the inn. Mr. Browne contended that Mr. Longton had no locus standti as the only persons who need appear before the court were the applicant for the transfer and the person who was leaving the house. Mr. Longton having obtained permission to state his objections contended that the transfer was taking place in an improper:and unjust'manner as regarded his client. When Mrs. Gorse died her will Nvas proved by his (Mr. Longton's) client. Afterwards a sale took place and Mr. Toft purchased goods to the amount of £4O which were unpaid for at the present time. Mr. Toft had been the licences for something like nine months and now he proposed to transfer the licence. Temporary authority was granted at the last Neavton Sessions and he (Mr. Longton) gave notice that he should oppose the transfer. ___

Mr. Browne: He tried to induce Mr. and Mrs. Toft to instruct him to do so and they absolutely refused. Mr. Longton: My friend is only lengthening my remarks. Continuing he said that when arrangements were being made for the transfer last week Mr. Toft and Mr. Butterworth each employed an auctioneer to make a valuation in the usual way. The result was that there was an amount exceeding £lOO to be paid to Mr. Toft. Mr. Brown: Nothing of the kind.

Mr. Lougt.on: My friend will contradict me and prove lam incorrect if he can. Mr. Toft continued Mr. Longton, signed a receipt for the money. He did not actually receive one penny. The brewery company were represented at the valuation and took the whole of the money. The amount owing for rent was a preferen- tial claim and the company had a perfect right to take it but in addition they pocketed the whole of the money which Mr. Toft ought to have received. Mr. Toft protested against his money being taken in that way because he had othee obligations to meet. The other creditors including tht executor were absolutely unpaid. Originally Mr. Tof instructed him (Mr. Longton) but there ho..d since been a change and Mr. Toft was now sailing in with Mr. Butterworth and the brewery company. His (Mr. Longton's) only locus standi was on behalf of the execu- tor and the other creditors who were unpaid.. The Chairman (Col. Ridgway): I don't think we have anything to do with it. Mr. Browne: My friend is trying to make you into a debt collecting agency. After further discussion the magistrates held that the only point for them to inquire into was the character of the applicant and as there was no objection to Mr. Butterworth on the ground of character the transfer was granted.

div.head: WIDNES FREE CHURCH COUNCIL AND THE EDUCATION ACT.
div.p: WIDNES FREE CHURCH COUNCIL AND THE EDUCATION ACT.

The Widnes Free Church Council have this week issued an appeal to "the free and independent citizens of Widnes.' It is respecting the action of the Widnes Town Council in the appointment of the new Education Committee, and signed with the names of the Rev. A. Harvey (president of the Council), the Rev. H. R. Williams and Mr. F. Lawrinson (hon. secretaries), and Mr. W. Wilcock (treasurer), and reads as follows : "We desire to bring before your notice the action of the majority of the Widnes Town Council on the 12th inst., in regard to the constitution of the New Educa- tion Committee. This committee is formed according to a scheme adopted by the Town Council, and sanc- tioned by the Board of Education, and is composed of twelve members of the Council, and eight outside, or ' co-opted ' members, viz.: One woman, one person nominated by the County oouncil, three nominated by the School Board, and one each by the Free Church Council, the Church of England Association, and the Roman Catholic Association. The intention was that the three members nominated by the School Board should represent each of the three parties on the Board—Mr. Evan Thomas being nomin- ated as representing Nonconformity. Without the faintest show of reason Mr. Thomas was rejected and Mr. J. J. Williams put.in his place, the pretext being that men of ability and experience were required on the tEducation Committee—a strange thing to urge against Mr.lThomas,who had been several years upon the School Board, where he had both gained experience and proved his ability as an educationalist. Mr. Thomas was also a representative Welshman, therefore his re- jection was manifestly unfair and invidious, besides leaving the important community of Welsh people amongst us without an exponent of their views. "Then, throwing to the wind the pretext upon which Mr. Thomas had been rejected, viz, that men of ex- perience and ability were required for the work of the new committee, Councillor Lewis (who had served 101 years on the School Board) and Councillor Davis were rejected in favour of Councillors Hurst and Midwood— gentlemen who, we believe, have no special fitness for the work, thus depriving the town of the services, upon this important committee of such a proved educa- tionalist as Councillor Lewis and such a tried public servant as Councillor Davies. "We have tried to understand the true meaning and import of this shameless attack. We do not wish to be majust, or to put blame where it is not due. But we have come to the conclusion that the onslaught is the outcome, mainly, of a compact between the worst forces 'of clerioalism OR the one hand, and the representatives of the drink traffic on the other; and is a direct blow not merely at the gentlemen concerned, but at Noncon- formity in general, andis in its nature a reprisal. "It was not our wish that the new Education Com- mittee should be sectarian in its composition, but the Town Council determined otherwise, and so that prin- ciple should have been faithfully carried out—due re- gard being given to educational efficiency. Fully one- third or more of the scholars in the elementary schools of the town are the children of Free Church parents ; therefore, on this ground it was only just and right that adequate representation should be accorded to Free Churchmen. "We do not, however, whine or repine at our lot. We are conscious that we are suffering in a good cause —the cause of the people. But, we should like to ask : Why should Nonconformity be attacked in this way? "We ask nothing for ourselves. We seek no special privileges. What,. then, is our offence? It is (1) that we insist on equality !—ft fair field and no favour ! (2) We advocate progress and efficiency in public management and administration. (3) We seek the freedom of civic life from the domination of the drink interest. - -

"We submit this fairly covers the ground of our action and aim in municipal affairs. We repeat that in this we do not seek any good peculiarly for ourselves, but the general wellbeing of the community. In proof of this we appeal to our record in public matters, and ask, have not representative Free Churchmen served the com- munity with ability and fairness? If this is so, and we submit it truthfully represents the facts, then this action of the majority of the Town Council is not. merely an affront to Nonconformity but an outrageous attack upon pure public policy, and a sacrifice of public interests in favour at sectarian preferences and the unworthy purposes of a clique. "We therefore appeal to all fair-minded citizens—by whom we believe, this disgraceful action will be con- demned—to actively interest themselves in municipal matters, and seek to secure such representatives that will honour their trust by promoting the public good, and so prevent a recurrence of conduct so compromis- ing to the public life of our town."

div.head: AUNT SOPHY.
div.p: AUNT SOPHY.
BY SHEILA ALISON,
Author of "The Surgeon's Wife," "Mayinff Harvest," "The Slip Knot," "A virti Woman," "Alas! Poor Ghost," "Her Astra Guardian," &e.

div.head: 1. -WHAT THE GIRLS SAID.
div.p: 1. -WHAT THE GIRLS SAID.
It is simple cruelty ! " mourned Amethyst. "If I were in the House of Commons," threatened Iseult, savagely, "I would cut down the Lord Chancellor's salary at once. I would abolish him altogether!"

"King Herod himself wasn't half so cruel," Amethyst went on, "to defenceless children. He did put them out of pain. He didn't send them to a nasty, cold, dark, lonely, barbarous place, to live under a sour-visaged spinster as gaoler, • where nobody could see them, and they could see nobody; and where nobody knew the difference between a Bond-street gown and one from the native modiste. All the pretty things I got for the Crickmays are wasted. Sackcloth would do for Long Chesterton 2" "Or blue paint," amended Iseult. "I don't suppose they have emerged from primeval _

"It is -such a waste," lamented Amethyst again. "Waste ! " cried Iseult. "It is perfectly shame- ful! Even a Lord Chancellor is supposed to have the country's interest at heart • he helps to govern it; and here he sends me, who feels inexhaustible power burning within me, and capacities for immense usefulness, to a stunted, shallow, stupid, uneducated village, where all that force will be simply lost !"_ _ _

"tO an old maid, too ! " groaned Amethyst. "She will think everything improper, and want us to read Miss Yonge's books all day, and knit stock- ings for the poor." "It shews how absurd it is that these offi9es should be invariably filled by men," said Iseult. "Now, a Lady Chancelloress would not have made such a pitifully absurd mistake as to send two girls liko us to the charge of an unsophisticated old maid, and not to a woman of the world and a mother like Aunt Crickmay."

div.head: H. -WHAT TILE VILLAGE SAID.
div.p: H. -WHAT TILE VILLAGE SAID.

"Poor dear Miss Ellaby What will she do with them? What havoc it will make in her house! How cruel of the Lord Chancellor to force such a fate upon her! Two modern girls from Girton, who will turn everything upside down, and make her life a burden to her. What will she say about it? What is she going to do with them? A hen in charge of ducklings has a peaceful time of it compared with what hers will be!" "She seemed a good deal dismayed, but she makes the best of everything, as usual. Amethyst, the elder one, is a great beauty, and not so very clever, though she was at Girton. Iseult is the clever one; goes in for woman's rights; would like to be a doctor, and that sort of thing. The Lord Chancellor took her quite by surprise. She didn't say so, of course, but the real reason must have been that Mrs. Crickmay is not a good chaperon for girls. She has been a good deal talked about, though I daresay she may have sobered down, as her own daughters are coming on." "What will be done about those girls? They will expect to be entertained and fussed over," said the vicar's wife.

"I promised to make a party for them," said her friend, Mrs. Medell, a naval Captain's widow. "Miss Ellaby means to invite us all, of course, for Thursday, the day after the girls come." "I suppose I shall have to have them," sighed the vicar's wife, Mrs. Heath; "but it really would be most inconvenient at present. I remember their mother, [think."
"They had two mothers. They are not sisters, thodgh they are both Kerrisons. Mary and Lucy Ellaby married brothers, and Grace Crickmay came next."

"And Sophy was the youngest? It seems quite odd. One always thinks of her as the eldest of everybody. I wonder why she never married?" "She never had an offer that anyone ever heard of. She was born to be an old maid. • She will make a capital dragon—keep off all undesirable lovers,"

div.head: 111. -WHAT THE GIRLS SAID.
div.p: 111. -WHAT THE GIRLS SAID.

"It was a delightful little party, Aunt Sophy," said Amethyst, "and so good of you to make it for us. The people are most amusing—kind, I mean. I suppose the golden youth of Long Chesterton shines chiefly at entertainments where more violent exercise is offered—balls, and tennis and water- parties ? " _ _

- "I am afraid, my dear, that our force of young men has passed before you to-night," Aunt Sophy answered, smiling amusedly. "They came eagerly, indeed, as they have never been known to come before, to see my two novelties.".
Amethyst looted honestly perplexed. Iseult said: "For myself, I prefer old men. The vicar, at least, was educated at Oxford. I don't want to flirt."

"Oh!" cried Amethyst, sarcastically. "You don't call it flirting, I suppose, when you monopolise old professors and young politicians for a whole even- ing; but it looks just the same. I suppose there isn't a Latin or Sanscrit word for flirting, or that would describe it perfectly." "Mr. Wood is not an old man," said Miss Ellaby. "He is only thirty-five and you cannot call Johnny Heath old, or FranliMedell—they are not out of their teens. There are never many men in the country. They are drafted away to towns." "There is the new member, Sir John Hendley. Don't you ever have him ?" asked Iseult. "Oh, my dear, he is too great a person to come to our little tea-parties. I don't even know him. He has only just come to the Hall. It has been shut up ever since his uncle died." "Then you should call upon, and invite him," said Amethyst. "It is very unkind to leave him out."
"My dear, he is a bachelor. I cannot possibly call upon him, or ask him to visit us. It would not. be proper. I believe he has called at the Vicarage." _
Amethyst sent a little twinkling glance from under her eyelashes at Iseult, but that young lady had laid aside her spectacles for the present; so it was lost.

Miss Ellaby seemed old enough to Amethyst to call upon a regiment, as far as propriety went. "I should like very much to know him," said Iseult, thoughtfully. -- "He is a very advanced Radical. I should like to talk to him about his property." "We are sure to meet him somewhere," continued she afterwards, when the cousins were in their own room brushing their hair; "and I will see that he is made free of the house. The only eligible creature here. We cannot afford to waste time."

div.head: IV.-WIIAT SIR JOHN SAID.
div.p: IV.-WIIAT SIR JOHN SAID.

"They are two remarkably pretty little girls! .Deliciously fresh, especially the dark one. I hope you will allow me to call upon you, Miss Ellaby, to improve their acquaintance," said Sir John. "He is a real tonic in this dead-level wilderness," said Amethyst to her cousin; "and I don't think he can be so very old. Anyway, his maturity stands out in most refreshing contrast beside the guileless infancies of the Heaths and Medells. I think, on the whole, I like old men best. They are kinder, politer, more chivalrous than the absurd creatures who call each other Johnnies and Chappies ; and who are always thinking so much about themselves and their looks, that they cannot spare a thought for other. people's." "He has some good ideas," said Iseult, thought- fully, as was her wont; "and he is not in the least bigoted, as very young Radicals often are. He likes to hear my views, and listens to them with the greatest attention; indeed, he is eager to draw me out. Some men might have preferred shutting me up. "Of course he enjoyed drawing her out," Amethyst said within herself. "I expect he has had no end of quiet fun to-night, thinking over what she has said. As if a man of his weight and experience would care for what a girl said! No, no! Men hate political and learned women. They like some- thing as different from themselves as possible. I knew he was talking about us all that time to Aunt Sophy, and now he is coming to call. I wonder when he will come, and whether I should wear white or a colour!"

"I see my way to a great career," mused Iseult, as she stared at the stars from her little white bed. "I am not mistaken; I am not the sort of girl who fancies every man who looks at her is in love with her, :for am I the girl a man would idly flirt with, much less draw out' for his private amusement. He talked to me nearly all the evening; he hardly dia more than stare at Amethyst; and I knew he etcl epeltMs-.rnato pun JOADIO tiOA II! 01:1 Imo ol 2ultuoe s! eti Atou pun 'upwind etn .tapun etug 21101 PTII4 qudoß luny 'al out lnoqu 2upunl SUM

he has his fads. These I can easily manage to make him give up. Why, a member of Parliament's wife is more than the member nowadays—." "Here comes Sir John!" exclaimed Amethyst. "What will our watchful dragon say, when she returns and finds what has happened? What fate inspired her to set off for the hospital so early? Destiny, Iseult—destiny He has certainly lost no time. Perhaps he saw her go out and seized the opportunity. Make haste, dear! I cannot go down to him quite unchaperoned." "As I am younger than you—" Iseult put it' hastily, flushing angrily. "Oh, as for that, we all on an equally unchaperoned level here, according to poor Aunt Sophy. We must chaperon each other." "I am sorry not to have found Miss Ellaby said Sir John, after shaking hands with the bright girls, each all shining in happy excitement, Iseult's brown eyes beaming behind her spectacles as radiantly as Amethyst's blue ones under her golden fringe. Both were in white, and Iseult :ad a bunch oi carnations in her dress.

"She won't be in until six," said Iseult, simply. Amethyst flashed an .angry glance at het cousin's unconscious back crop of dark hair—she wore hers gathered into a fluffy golden heap on the top of her head. "She may be in any minute," she contradicted. "How stupid of Iseult not to remember that Sir John, being so old, might have antiquated English ideas as to the propriety. of prolonging his visit when the dragon was off auty 1 "Well, I hope you will manage to take care of me till she comes," said Sir John.

Iseult was rather annoyed at his manner, which savoured somewhat of the caressing patronage he might have used to children—and rather perplexed, too; and her consequent pause, and then a moment of deliberation, whether first to introduce the subject of Irish land or of Welsh tithes, gave Amethyst her. opportunity. _ _
"W4;'ll take' the best of care. Come into the garden and eat strawberries. We will pick them, and then eat them in the corner, under the copper- beech."

"You don't care for strawberries ? " said Iseult, gravely, to Sir John. How could anybody discuss land and tithes, stooping over strawberry-beds, and impeding the utterance of every other word by a strawberry surreptitiously popped into one's mouth? But Sir John elected for the strawberries, and Iseult could but bide her time and wait an oppor- tunity. She had it when, an hour later, they were sitting at the rustic table under the copper- beech with their strawberries and cream.

"I suppose you have hardly had time to see the Premier's speech at Cardiff yet, the papers are so late coming here," she said. Sir John had paired for the rest of the session with the Tory member for another division, as he had important business to look after at home. _ _
"How can you tease about politics on such a lovely afternoon ? " cried Amethyst. "Do let us enjoy our strawberries ! " _

Bt Sir John evidently was not teased by politics, nor hindered by them from enjoying the straw- berries. He seemed immensely interested in discuss- ing these great questions with Iseult, and even took pains to keep Amethyst well placed in the conversation, and made the topics quite amusing and interesting, so that she might not be bored, and was even led into giving her own opinions on the subjects discussed. _

"He -is glad of any excuse to stay on with us," she thought. At six o'clock Miss Ellaby returned, and was sent by the servant to find the merry party under the copper-beech. The stiawberries were all eaten; but Sir John insisted on gathering .more. And just to soften any wrath that might lie hidden under her gentle exterior, because he had stayed so long, he actually stayed on till seven o'clock; and then Miss Ellaby virtually hinted him off the premises, by asking him to stay to tea, as it was their hour.

"No, thanks; I must be off r* he exclaimed, starting up guiltily and looking quite sorry. "I have paid an unconscionable visitation; but, in fact, I waited for you, Miss Ellaby, so it is your fault. I want to give a party of some sort—a sort of house-warming, in fact, or garden-warming, if there is such a thing, for these young people will want tennis; and I thought you would advise me what to have and who to have."
Amethyst literally jumped for joy. "But I must not detain you," continued Sir John. "May I come again, Miss Ellaby, to talk it over?"

The vicar: "Her dress seems to me perfection, for it is perfectly suitable to her age an circum- stances. She dresses like a modest gentlewoman. As for Miss Kerrison's dress, it is, no doubt, pretty and fashionable, but I "declare I blushed when she came into the room last night, and hardly could bear to glance in her direction all the even- ing. Her other dresses seem to me too smart for this country place." Mrs. Medell : "Her evening dresses are certainly hardly decent." The vicar: "Then, do you admire Miss Iseult's dress? I declare I nearly called after her the other day, thinking it was you, Frank." Edith Lee;" She is very masculine; it is horrid." Johnny: "but her hats, and ulster, and little natty coats all fit her so bewitchingly. A pretty girl may wear anything she likes." Miss Bowen: "There is nothing so repulsive to me as an unwomanly woman." Mrs. Heath: "I daresay she is pure womanly enough to be very glad to catch a baronet. He seems to like her style, since he is pulling the place to pieces to please her." Mrs. Modell: "She is not the rose, but near the rose. It is an excuse to get near Amethyst to go to the White louse with plans of drains and ventilators.'

Alice Heath: "Amethyst certainly thinks he is in love with her. She blushed when I mentioned him the other day, and she could hardly attend to anything last night when we were all expecting him, and then she smiled when he came, and appropriated him at once."
Edith Lee: "Why, Iseult talks as if they were already married. She says, 'we ' shall have this done, and ' we' object to the other. It is perfectly absurd."

Chimes : "Well, time will shew very soon now. He has abundance of opportunity, and not even a pretence at ignorance of his pretensions to contend with or a show of coyness. Elegant females' do not seem to think it due to themselves to refuse a man the first time he offers, as they did in Miss Austen's days. His mouth is open, and they are both ready to drop in, and no doubt he will be equally happy with either. It is only a matter of which dear charmer happens to be out of the way when the spirit, moves him to propose."

VI. -WHAT AMETHYST SAID (TO HER REFLECTION). "To-morrow I shall wear my black dress! lam almost sure that I look best in black, after all. Black is a very good idea. He has seen me in nothing but white and light things, and, perhaps, as men are so blind, they seem all alike to him; and men do require novelty. Who knows but that my sudden appearance in black may startle him into saying something more definite—more official, I should say; for he could hardly have made his meaning plainer, really. Perhaps he hesitates, thinking I am too young to be married and settle down to an important and influential position. I shall look more sedate and more like a stately Lady Hendley in black. . . . Aunt Sophy is a hope- less old maid. I told Sir John how she actually expected I would have helped her with her nasty, infectious hospital, and go poking into those horrid cottages, .and stay in the house this lovely weather to smother myself beneath heaps of hot flannel for the poor. He said so nicely that some people were born to be butterflies, and we should not like to do without them, useless as they are ; which I dare- say punished Aunt Sophy nicely, saying as it did that she was an ant, grubbing down amongst the dust and sand. I must say for Aunt Sophy that, in spite of her antiquated notions, she has taken to effacing herself a good deal lately. I think she will be sorry to part with me."

div.head: V. -WIIAT TILE VILLAGE SAID.
div.p: V. -WIIAT TILE VILLAGE SAID.

Omnes: "There must certainly be something in it. The question is, what, or, rather, which ? " Mrs. Heath: "Iseult. He has promised to have a Home Rule demonstration in his park to please her, and he is going to pull down the Colter's-row cottages, and build a hideous new place, like a workhouse, instead, after a design she has drawn." Mrs. Medell: "No; Amethyst. A man turns to beauty like flies to honey. He is far too practical with Iseult to be in love with her. When people are in love, they don't talk about drains and Acts of Parliament."

Mrs. Heath: "It certainly is Iseult. He treats Amethyst like a baby, and laughs at her little airs. A man doesn't laugh at a girl he is in love with." Miss Bowen: "It is neither one nor the other— not in that way. He is dull, and he has found two girls ready to flirt with him, and pet him; and he is willing enough to accept their homage, like any other idle man." Mrs. Medell: "No; that cannot be. He is a gentleman, and as clever and practical as he is kind. He would never keep going to the White House, day after day, knowing how ready girls are to misconstrue mild people to talk, unless he had honourable intentions."

Alice Heath: "Amethyst is 'rasaly in love with him. Iseult is far too high up in the clouds to think of love." Edith Lee: "No; Iseult is as much in love as any ordinary young woman. Amethyst treats him like a grandfather. He could not care for a butterfly thing like her. Iseult and he are twin souls—kindred spirits." _ .

Mrs. Medell;' "As for kindred spirits, men always marry their opposites." Miss Bowen: "It is rather hard on the Long Chesterton girls that these Kerrisons should have come. If they had stayed away, what a chance it would have been for Clara Scott! She is exactly the girl that would have suited him." _
Mrs. Heath: "He doesn't seem to see it. He never looks at her."
Alice Heath: "Amethyst has got a new con- signment of dresses from Bond-street. The Lord Chancellor really ought to interfere. Her bills must be outrageous 1" _

Edith Lee: `‘The Lord Chancellor is a Tory. He will never allow the wedding to take place." Mrs. Heath: "Perhaps that is why Iseult is so rapturous about the recent elections and the Unionist split. She wants a Liberal Lord Chancellor to come in."

Johnny Heath: "I never heard such stuff! As if either of them would look at an old fogey like that ! The two jolliest girls that ever, came near the place!" Frank Medell: "Iseult might have him; she's not jolly ; she's an awful prig, just like yourself— but Amethyst! By Jove! A man would deserve to be banished from the country who proposed to mono-pelise her. Did you ever see such eyes, and such dimples, and such glorious hair ? And the way that girl can play tennis, why, it's divine!" Mr. Wood: "Miss Kerrison is very charming, but in my opinion Miss Iseult is far more beautiful. She has the %face of St. Catherine—or, rather, of Hypatia, since I fear her Christianity is not her strong point. If she would but suffer herself to be taught by those appointed to teach her, what might aot her talents, her enthusiasm, her self-devotion, do for the Church? She would he thrown away by marriage. I feel sure that she at least is not a willing attraction for Sir John." The vicar: "They are pretty girls, hut neither of them is to be compared with their aunt. Oh, yes, you boys may stare, but Sophy Ellaby was ten times prettier than they are when she was a girl; and she has hardly lost any of her beauty. Her grey hair is as pretty as theirs, and her tomplexion is as good, and her soft eyes could never lose their expression ; and, with all Miss Iseult's tall talk, I should like to see her do half as much with her wh.qe life as her aunt has done with every year of hers. As for conversation, I never knew a better, more sympathetic and intelligent listener than Miss Ellaby, and she has a wonderful gift of seeming to have said almost nothing, and yet to have placed things in a clearer light for you." Mrs. Lee: "But there is no room for compari- son; the girls are girls, and quite different from elderly people; have less experience, of course, and are apt to overdo enthusiasm." The vicar: "She is far younger than they are, though her hair turned white a little after she was thirty. Her manner seems to me (mite child- ueide liss iierrison's vanity woman-of-the-worldisliness, and Miss Iseult's learned theorising." Alice Heath: "She is a regular old frump. Look at her dress!"

div.head: VII. -WHAT ISEULT SAID (TO lIER JOURNAL).
div.p: VII. -WHAT ISEULT SAID (TO lIER JOURNAL).

"I see exactly where his fault is. He is full of right ideas, and eager to improve himself and to assimilate mine, and not at all bigoted about giving ttp plans that I condemn; but he has a want of practicality. He is too sublimated, as it were, about some things. He doesn't seem to know that though we understand each other perfectly well, our position would be strengthened if, in fact, we were officially engaged. It seems to him needless, since our souls are in perfect union, to attempt to deepen and strengthen that union by conventional forms. That shews how a woman's practical mind comes in to steady and guide a man's. He recognises our perfect equality so fully that I believe it has not occurred to him that the initiative should be with him any more ~than with me—in fact, it strikes me that he will not presume to speak since I do not, his natural chivalry yielding precedence to a woman, and that he waits for me. . . .I will give him until after the demonstration ; if he., has not spoken by then, two more days hence, I will speak. . It is rather tiresome that Amethyst is so often in the way, but he is wonderfully patient with her. Still, I wish she could be as sensible as Aunt Sophy and keep out of the way more, now she must see how things are. Perhaps Aunt Sophy would be less ready to efface herself if he did not tease her about her Toryism. She is very old- maidish—she makes such a fuss if my papers are what she calls littering about when visitors come. She looks gloomily at us sometimes. I suppose she sees all her pet fads and theories knocked down when I come into power at the Hall."

div.head: VIII. -WIIAT SIR JOHN SAID
div.p: VIII. -WIIAT SIR JOHN SAID

"But I cannot understand. I mean, how was it possible you did not understand? I flattered myself that a man had never been more straight- forward. Why, I have hardly ever been out of the house. lam quite ashamed to think how I must have bored you, but you have been too kind. You not only hid from me that you were bored, but you seemed to encourage me by your—by looking pleased to see me, and all that. You are the only person in the parish who has not understood. Everyone else seems to have guessed that I could not come here so often for mere friendship's sake." "But the girls—it might have been the girls." "The girls " in genuine incredulous astonish- ment.

"They are so pretty, and Iseult. is so clever. They would be so much more suitable." "Suitable! Good Heavens! Which one? Little Amethyst, with her dimples and baby nonsense, or Iseult, with her blue-books and spectacles ? " "You seemed to enjoy the blue-books and the nonsense very much
"I enjoyed anytious;thai kept me near you." "Iseult would enter i4to all your plans and ambi- tions."
"She would do nothing of the sort... She would insist on my going in for hers. She is a pretty little goose, and it is charming to hear her wild theories."

"I am a 'Tory! I pauperise the poor! I can't bear to think of the pretty old cottages coining down. lam an old maid with antiquated notions, and my hair is white, and I have no sympathy with the revolutionary spirit." "Sophy, you are the most beautiful, and the sweetest, and cleverest, and womanliest, and youngest of women." "I am forty-one." "And I am forty two; a very proper age for you. The world is upside down now, I think; and girls are born twenty years old. Both these girls are old enough and wise enough—for little Amethyst is the wiser of the two, with real practical world-wisdom —to be your great-aunts. Sophy, I am sure yoa care for me. Will you be my wife ? "
IX. -WHAT AUNT WPM( sAm. "Yes; I suppose so. lam afraid people will be surprised."

X.-WHAT THE GIRLS SAID. "I knew she would be jealous of us, and set him trainst us, wicked old thing!" "He thinks she has money. He would be jealous )f a wife who took the lead. He is very narrow, after all, very prejudiced, and cannot submit to being ruled by a woman. He wants a tool." _
_ "After all, it will be very nice to live at the Hall till we are married."
"A woman can never be free and supreme if she binds herself down by marriage. I shall be far more the power at the Hall than if I had been his wife."

div.head: XT.-WHAT THE TILLAGE SAID.
div.p: XT.-WHAT THE TILLAGE SAID.

"It is ye y astonishing, but really much wiser; and Sophy Eilaby is a very pretty woman, and much more 'suitable to be lady of the Manor than a little extravagant flirt, or a young woman who wants to inture upon the franchise, and to wear a &Sided F kirt, as she calls it."

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
St. James's, Latchford.

The services at this church on Whit-sunday were of a festal character befitting the occasion and there were good congregations. The preacher at the morning ser- vice, 'which was well sung to Berthold Tours in C, was the Rev. H. A. Lester, M.A., Warrington Training College. In the evening the Viear (the Rev. F. R. Pearson, M.A.) was the preacher. Dr. Bunnett's Magnificat and Nunc Dimitis in F were sung, while the rendering of the anthem "I will pour out my spirit," by Dr. Cuthbert Harris, was distinctly credit- able. Mi. J. Hill ably sang the opening bass solo, Miss B. Eckersley was heard to advantage in the soprano solo, while the trio was beautifully interpreted by Miss tckersley and Messrs.J. Pevitt and J. Hill. Mr. E. Davies, F.V.C.M. presided at the organ.

div.head: Emmanuel Reformed Church.---Interesting Presentation.
div.p: Emmanuel Reformed Church.---Interest- ing Presentation.

There was an interesting gathering in connection With this church the other evening when the congrega- tion assembled to formally welcome the Rev. A. G. D. Gee as minister of the church. Mr. William Parsons,of Moore, presided, and in well-chosen words voiced the teeling of the meeting, as did also Mr. Henry Gandy, and Mr. William Dickens (people's wardens).—The Rev. A. G. D. Gee, who was enthusiastically received,thanked the congregation for their cordial welcome. He spoke of the unique characteristics of Warrington, owing to its situation and the great diversity of its trades. He EWA that owing to this there must, of necessity, be differences of -opinion, which, however, ought not to lead to personal disagreements. Each ought to look Charitably on the opinions of the other, remembering always the accountability of every man to God alone-- 31usical items were contributed during the evening by Miss Elsie Gandy, Miss Heywood, and the choir, Mrs. Arthur Landon officiatingat the piano. Much pleasure ....Was also afforded by a recitation competition, of which !qrs. Walter Myles and Mrs. Gee were easy winners.— ring an interval occasion was taken to present Mr. "leery Gandy with a salad bowl and cruet as amark of affection and appreciation of his long and faithful services to the church. Mr. Parsons made the presenta- tion, and reminded the meeting that the recipient had been connected with the church from its incep- tion, and only relinquished his active work bow because the exigencies of business de- manded his removal from Warrington. Mr. Gandy, in thanking the meeting, stated that he was too much surprised and overcome to adequately express his feelings, but so far as his work was concerned he could say that he had always been encouraged by the thotight that whatever he did, however little, it was something towards the maintenance of those Protestant Principles in which he had been nurtured, and for which the Emmanuel Church stood.—The conclusion of his remarks was greeted by the singing of "He's a jolly Rood fellow."—Votes of thanks were accorded to the 1;111am-ism and those who contributed to the success of the gathering.
