div.head: MUNICIPAL TRADING AND INVESTORS.
div.p: MUNICIPAL TRADING AND INVESTORS.

No doubt the memorial addressed to the Bank of I England by the Industrial Fieedom League is well meant, says Mr. Charles Duguid in this week's issue of "The World," and it is certainly most influentially signed. The title Industrial Freedom League seems suggestive of Oddfellows or something of the sort; but Lord Avebury is the president of the League, and seeing that the circular is signed by more than a hundred and fifty gentlemen, including Lord Claud Hamilton, Lord Stalbridge, Mr. Vicary Gibbs, Sir Clinton Dawkins,and Mr. Herbert Spencer, to take only a few names at ran- dom, it is not a document likely to be disregarded. It draws the attentica of the Bank of England to the remarkable disposition which our local authorities have undoubtedly shown recently to freely borrow money in the market by the issue of Corporation loans. The tendency to increase these loans is deplored by the memorialists, who respectfully submit that the borrow- ing should be discouraged when the money is sought for trading purposes, and that even when the loans are not issued for that purpose they should be kept within prudent limits. Nobody is going to dispute with the Industrial Freedom League over the necessity of keeping loans, whether issued by oorp)ra- tions or Governments, or even individuals, within prudent limits, whatever those limits may be. Nor can it be denied that the lavishness with which municipal authorities have recently been borrowing and, accord- ing to appearances, are likely to continue to borrow suggests some imprudencd. Further, it is true, as the memorialists point out, that many local authorities are embarking with the money they borrow upon schemes, such as tramwayand electric-lighting schemes, whicha eof a somewhat speculative nature. There is no doubt that the competition with private enterprise which this policy involves forms the main reason for the agitation against municipal loans by the memorial- I ists of the Industrial Freedom League. The name of , the League sufficiently implies its objects. It isa League to free those engaged in our industries from I rate-aided competition. It is not a League to protect ! the investor against the danger of lending money to our , cerponttions, and therefore it is not called the In- vestors' Protection League. . .

This being the case, it appears to be rather disingen- uous on the part of the League to approach such an institution as the Bank of England on the plea that these Corporation loans are becoming dangerous to the investor. What the League really wants is to stop municipal trading, and this •object may be very desir- able, and doubtless Nis But instead of frankly admitt- ing this, the League tries to prevent the municipal aathorities borrowing money by raising the bogey of insecurity. If the policy of commercial adventure, say the memorialist, is continued it will greatly increase the amount of the loans, and seriously affect the charac- ter of municipal stocks. Trading Enterprises they argue of an experimental nature are unsuited for the investment of municipal funds, especially having regard to the fact that the stocks of the larger cities are authorised trustee investments. Because the memorial- ists are rather disingenuous in the method they are adopting to check municipal trading they fall into a fallacy, as is usually the case in such circumstances—a f<illacy which is all the more remarkable considering the status of the gentlemen who sign the document. They try to make out thatithis municipal trading is a danger to the investor who supplies the money to carry it on, while the truth is that it is a danger nut to them,but to the rate- payers, upon whose money the loans are secured. Such gentlemen as those whose names have just been men- tioned must surely know that if the commercial ad- vliture proves a failure it is not the investor and the j.trllltee who will lose the money; it is the ratepayer, who will have to find it in order to pay off the investor both as regards interest and principal. Of course, if one has an imagination wild enough one can dream of a day when the last penny of the ratepayer's money has been torn from his pocket. so that there is nothing left with which the municipality can repay its indebtedness to the investor ; in other words, when our corporations shall reach the end of their rating power, and shall be compelled to default and become bankrupt because the inhabitants are unable to pay more rates Practically speaking, such a picture I is, of course, absurd, but until such a time arrives trustees and investors are perfectly well secured, in spite of the- alarm which these memorialists to the Bank of England desire to sow among them. Their attempt to check reckless municipal trading commands sympathy, but if they desire to accomplish it straightforwardly they should address themselves,not to the Bank of England— is the Bank of England to refuse to issue Corporation loans ?—and to trustees and investers, but to the rate- payers themselves. At all events while the trustee and the investor may deplore as much as the Industrial Freedom League does the modern tendency towards municipal trading—what does the League say as to the intention of the New Zealand Government to open butchers' shops ?—they need not regard its warning as to the insecurity of their stocks with much anxiety. Long before any English corporation defaults in its obligations to its stockholders its ratepayers, however j apathetic, will have been compelled by the weight of Itheir rates to arise and make a clean sweep of those who are :3peculating at a loss with their money.

div.head: Runaway Horse in Wilderspool-road.
div.p: Runaway Horse in Wilderspool-road.

Excitement was created by an accident which occurred in Wilderspool-road shortly before noon on Monday. An invalid phaeton belonging to Mr. T. H. Lyon, Appleton Ball, was being driven- along Wilderspool Causeway, near St. James's Church, by a man named John Cooper, when a passing tramcar caused the pony to become restive, and it bolted. The phaeton collided with one of the wooden frames pro- tecting the trees on the side of the road, and the driver was thrown out. The affrighted animal then dashed along the Causeway, but luckily there was no further accident. Edward Bate, the driver of a tramcar coming in the opposite direction, seeing the pony daSh- ing along, brought his car to a standstill,and,with the assistance of Mr. Alfred Jolley, succeeded in stopping the animal. The phaeton, however, was completely smashed. The driver, as the result of his fall, sus- tained a lacerated wound on his elbow, and " first-. aid " was rendered by Police Constable Reddington A Haydock Pastor's Work.

The work of the Rev. J. H. Riddette, who has been pastor of the Haydock Congregational Church since it was built by the late Miss Ruth Evans, twelve years ago. is. very favourably reviewed in this month's Liverpool and district " Congregational Magazine," which also k,Tives Mr. Riddette's portrait. Internally, the church is exceedingly handsome, and the rostrum is a finely-executed piece of -work. The cost of the church, schools, and minister's house was £9,000. Miss Evans made herself responsible for the minister's support, and her purpose was that the church should hecothe a centre of economic, social, and educational work, as well as work distinctly spiritual. Her heart was set on a church and ministry which should elevate , he tastes, brighten the lives, and build up the char- acters of the mining population, In Mr. .Riddette, with his wide outlook and social sympathies and fear- lessnesS in grappling with great problems, coupled with -earnestness in preaching the ,Gospel, Miss Evans made a wise selection. Unfortunately, her ' ' death placed the church and affiliatad institutions in a! critical condition. The struggle for life through which the church had to pass for some years ended in good to all. It welded the people more compactly together, , and there emerged a most healthy and vigorous church A mere enumeration of the activities at Hay- dock will be sufficient to prove that the founder's , ideals are being loyally and succassfully carried out , under Mr. Riddette's leadership, for excellent work is, being done by the men's club, with a useful library, men's and women's tontine, women's meeting, band of hope, and Young People's Society for Christian Endeavour. A recent mission resulted in increased membership. Mr. Riddette, who is splendidly sup- ported by an able wife, is a thorough-going Congrega- tionalist, and has published a "Catechism of Con- gregational Church Principles," which has been com- mended by very high authorities. Mr. ltiddette gave great assistance to the colliers among whom he lives during the privations of the great strike. Until a short time ago he represented the tywnship on the War- rington Board of Guardians and his devotion during the critical times above referred to is now bearing fruit in the community.

The Liverpool Stipendiary (Mr. J. W. Stewart) on Monday disposed of 186 cases at Dale-street Police Courb in an hour and a half. His Worship wanted a holiday, but his clerical staff were kept busy for a couple of hours after he had gone in an endeavour to get level with him in his race through the calendar.

div.head: OLD WARRINGTON. HOW THE TOWN APPEARED
div.p: OLD WARRINGTON. HOW THE TOWN APPEARED

It is on reading a description of Warrington as it appeared nearly a hundred years ago that one realizes the great changes that have taken place with the industrial progress of the town. This week we have been shown A ,toplgraphical dictionary of the United Kingdom; compiled from Parliamentary and other authentic documents and authorities; contain- ing geographical, topographical and statisticas. accounts of every district object and place in England, Wales, Scotland, Ireland, and the various small islands dependant on the British empire" which was printed in 1808. The information was coraiiled by Benjamin Phipps Capper, Esq., and the pr nitr of the volume was J. G. Barnard, Snow Hill. The follow- ing is the description of Warrington : WARRINGTON, a market town and parish in the hundred of West Derby, Lancaster, 11 miles from Northwich, on the banks of the Mersey, which separ- ates it from Cheshire and 173 miles from London; containing 2,258 houses and 10,567 inhabitants, viz. : 4,780 males and 5,787 females, of whom 4,056 were employed in various trades and manufactures, par- ticularly sail-cloth, canvas, fustian, pins, glass, &c. The streets are open and contain handsome modern buildings, while others are long and narrow, contain- ing mean houses, especially at the entrance of the town. The church contains many ancient and Wind- some monuments, and it has a neat chapel of ease, con- secrated in 1760. This town has an excellent free grammar school; it has also a large and elegant building, being an academy for the education of , youth, particularly in trade and merchandise. Here are also two charity-schools, the ore for clothing and leducating 24 boys; the other for 26 boys, endowed and founded by a Mr. Waterson, who procured the money by the exhibition of a dancing horse in various parts of the country. Over the river Mersey is a hand- some stone bridge, near which anciently stood a priory of Augustines. Th.e river produces excellent fish. Besides its manufactures of Huckabacks and coarse cloths, Warrington has long it noted for the excel- lence of its malt, in which t carries on considerable traffic. It is not incorporated, but is governed ! by the justices of the peace, assisted by four constables. Here is a bank. Market on Wednesday, noted for fish, provisions, and all kinds of cattle, not inferior to the Leicestershire breed. Fairs, 18th July and 30th November, which last a week each. The church is a rectory, rated at 40s. The volume contains a map of Lancashire on which Newton is more prominently marked than Warrington. The town, it appears, was then known as Newton in the Willows, and in the dictionary it is described as a borough town and chapelry in the parish of Win- wick, hundred of West Derby, Lancaster, four and a half miles from Warrington, and 179 from London, containing 178 houses and 1,455 inhabitants, of t. whom 356 were returned as being employed in various trades. This was once a market - town, but the market is now discontinued although the market cross is still standing in the Church yard. It is a borough by prescription, and is governed by a steward, bailiff and burgesses, and has returned two members to parliament since the first year of Queen Elizabeth; the right of election is supposed to be in the free burgesses. The returning officers are the steward of the lord of the manor and the bailiff. It has two charity schools, with a con- siderable manufacture of fustian and Manchester goods. Fairs, 17th May and 11th August, very con- siderable for horned cattle. Here is a Chapel of ease to the mother church."

div.head: MR. ROBERT DAVIES'S RECOLLECTIONS.
div.p: MR. ROBERT DAVIES'S RECOLLECTIONS.
Public Education and the Speech and Dialect of Warrington People.

In an interesting series of recollections of War- rington by the late Mr. Robert Davies, which are being printed in "The Dawn," there appears in the month's issue some of his recollections of the public education and the speech and dialect of the people of Warrington, in the early part of last century. He says :

When I first recollect Warrington there were so far as I recollect no schools of a public character for the education of the people beyond the Grammar School, the Blue Coat School, the Ladies School for girls and the Sunday Schools. The Grammar School was en- tirely free except the payment of five shillings a quarter which was paid (as popular tradition had it) for cocks to be tied up and thrown at by the boys. I think at Shrove Tide, but as a classical education was com- pulsory under the terms of the School's foundation comparatively few availed themselves of its advan- tages. Now that free scholarships at the School are open to the best boys from elementary schools, a new era has beguß, and an opportunity is afforded to boys possessed of &inlay to fit themselves for the learned professions, or for the numerous official appointments dependent on the results of examinations open to all. The Blue Coat School received a certain number of boys and girls into the house, and many in Warring- ton are indebted to that institution for a start in life. There was a day school in connection with it in my early day. . _

Tlie adios school has done admirable work in pro- I viding education for girls, and was and still is situated at the easterly end of Mersey-street near the "Running pump," which stood there, but never ran water in my days. I have been frequently told in the course of my life that all the education my informants had had was from the Sunday school. My own father and my wife's fatherand myself in my turn were teachers in them,and , although for the mere A B C education Sunday schools I have been superseded by the modern education system there can be no doubt that such schools have been and are still of infinite benefit. In my own case, I went first to a dame's school to learn my letters, and then to a master who kept a mixed private school for further advancement, and who grounded us well in Lindley's English grammar and spelling, writing from dictation, arithmetic, the elements of book-keeping, and general subjects including the elements of history, geography, and even astronomy, so far as to give his pupils an idea of the solar system. From him I went to the Grammar school, and thence to Rugby. I mention these facts merely to give my readers an accurate idea of educa- tion which then prevailed. I may ad'l that the Rev. I W. J. Beamont, who died Senior Fellow of Trinity College, and many others of that age had a precisely similar education. It may be supposed that many at that time could neither read nor write. In my father's canvas workshops bundles of tallies were kept on which the foreman cut notches for the bobbins that were spun, the bundles of yarn given out, and the number of pieces of canvas brought in by the weavers. Employers, as I have already mentioned generally " thoud " and " theed " their workpeople, and it was considered more as a mark of familiarity than of disrespect. The workpeople all used the same form of speech so each other, though not to their employers. The French and Germans still use this form only, I think, to their relatives and familiar friends. The letter "h" was, as in German, French,and Italian, entirely ignored, not, as sometimes happens now, inserting the aspirate in the wrong place in their I endeavours to speak "genteelly" (as they would ex- press it.) Under the gradual influence of education many old fashions of speech, and many then familiar common words and phrases are dying away. "A'thissuns " and "a'thattuns " for "this Way" and "that way" "th'owd lad" for the devil; "running gill men" for frequent tipplers; "badgers" for corn and dealers; "sWalers " for persons who go round the country and buy from farmers; .`scowbanks" and "scowbankers" for street corner men; ,"skewwifter" for a worthless man; "what the hnngment " (in Nor- wegian or Swedish "oh! the hangman") a kind of semi-oath: 'chastise " for "scold"; " bullyragging" for " bullying "; "the fold" for "the yard;" "two- thry " fora few," two-three- "twothry apples ; " throw- ing "heaving ; " "knotting pins," heading pins with loose heads of twisted brass wire (work often done by women in cottages) ; "knobstick,"•one who works over- time or refuses to join a strike (e.g. "thou'rt knobstick- ing, thou art"); "gradely" for "properly," (e.g. do it "gradely," "thou'rt a gradely foo'); " "like a brass , knocker on a nigsty door" for anything incongruous, I (e.g. "that mon put a brass knocker oat' pigsty door"); "neverbelike" for "never, surely,"; "under I the bongs" for Mersey-street (query, "under the banks ") ; " welly " for " wel in igh " (e.g. " welly drunk);" "crewdling down" for "cowering down;" "traycle batty" for "bread spread with treacle;" "singlet" for waistcoat; "dither" for " tremble," e.g. "I'm all on a dither ; " "lommering" for "climbing clumsily ; " and "lungeous" for ill-tempered and ready to lunge out v • ainst anyone with a stick, or weapon. The word lommering " brings to my mind a tale of an old widower, who was taking farewell of a dying parishioner. "John," said he, "when you get to heaven,yoo must try and find my wife." "Ay," said the poor fellow, "but I'm lame, and how can I go lommering all o'er heaven for t'look for her!: This provokes another story. When Mr. Hornby was rector and squire of 'Winwick, worth about £3,000 a year until he and the patron got an Act to divide the parish, he had been reading from the book of Revelation about the new Jerusalem to a very old tenant farmer of his. Seeing the farmer rather apathetic, the Rector reminded him of what he had been reading, and asked him if he did not wish to go there. The old man agreed that it must be very beautiful, "but, Mester Hornby, owd Winnick for me." Like Tennyson's Lincolnshire farmer, he had done his duty by "th' lend" and did not wish to leave it.

WISE men make proverbs for fools to follow. A AN is known by the photographs he keeps. Tis verage man thinks he is above the average. NATURAL TO ASK.—" They say he is a natural born genius." "Who supports him? ' A MAN is as old as he feels; a woman as old as she tells. A CYNIC is a man who will laugh at anything so long as it isn't humorous. IN LIK K CASE.—A: "I don't mind the influenza itself—it's the after-effect afrai,i or." B:

"The after-effect is what ails me. I'm dodging the doctor for two guineas at the present time." " WHAT was Nero's great crime ?" asked the teacher of a history class. "He played the fiddle," replied Sammy Wiffles. MAN (to angler): "Have you caught anything, guv'nor ?" Angler: "Of course not! I'm not a fisherman; I'm an angler." JACK (tenderly, to the little brother of his adored one) : "Would you like to know a secret, Tommy?" Tommy: "Should think I would." Jack : " Well, I'm in love with your sister." Tommy: "Oh, that's no secret. The family has talked about it every day since Aunt &null promised Nell that she'd bring about an introduc- tion."

BRIDE (throwing hetr arms about the bridegroom's neck) : "You are my prisoner for life." Bride- groom: "It's not imprisonment for life, love; it's capital punishment." A BROAD HlNT.—Viwitor : "Is Mies Rose at home? " Servant : "No, sir." Visitor: " Why, she has just come in ! I saw her." Servant : "Yes, sir; and she saw you, too." SHE: "You ought to be ashamed of yourself, John, for shooting such a dear little bird." He: "I thought you would like it for your hat."—She: "Oh, what a good idea! That was very thoughtful of you, John." HUSBAND: "It seems to me that you come to my office a good deal more than there is any necessity for." Wife : "I cannot help it dear ; your manners in the office are so much nicer than they are at home, that I like to enjoy the contrast." "WHY did you break off your engagement with Miss Bertha?" "Because her parrot was always saying, Stop that, George !" "But what differ- ence did that make? Your engagement was not a secret." "But my name is not George." PROVED.—" No," said Mr. Rockwell, as he wiped his glasses, "I'm afraid John's college education isn't going to do him much good after all." " Why, William," his anxious wife cried, "what makes you say that?" "He admitted in the shop yesterday that there were still a few things I knew more about than he did." UNCLE EBEN'S PHILOSOPHY.—" Dar am' no good o' being backward in dis life," said Uncle Eben. "Dc parrot ain't a very smaht bird, but it manages purty comfortable jes' by gittin' on de pert& an' hollerin' de little bit it knows." IN DAYS OF OLD.—The official bulletin of the War Department read as follows: "A dispatch has just been received from Ctesar. He says, Veni, vidi, vici.'" The Roman people were plainly annoyed. "Why in Tartarus doesn't he send particulars '?" they asked in one voice. AN UNLOOKED-FOR TiFv.—She "Did you say they had a tiff and the engagement was broken off?" : "Yes, but the tiff came after it was broken off. In fact, she was it—the plain-tiff in the action for breach of promise." MRS. BUMMER: "Has your husband any pet names for you?" Mrs. Slimmer: Oh, yes !" Mrs. Bummer: "What are they?" Mrs. Slim- mer : "Urn—to tell the truth, the names he calls me when he is in a pet are hardly of the kind that I care to repeat." LANDLADY: "Well, I must do something to keep the wolf from the door." Boarder: "I don't know that it is altogether necessary. Let hien come in and partake of one uf your breakfasts, and I don't think he'll trouble you again." A TEACHER asked a little boy to spell "respon- sibility," which he did. "Now, Tommy, said the teacher, "can you tell me the meaning ot that big word ? " " Yis, mum," answered TOITIOI7. "Ii I had only four buttons on my trousers, and two came off, all the responsibility would hang on the other two." GROWN-UP WOMEN.—"C!ara," raid the e o' lier of a litle tive.yeal-old mimiss, w:)u was er,tertaa.lmg a couple of neighbouring girls of her own age, •' why don't you play something instead of sitting still and looking miserable ? ' "Why, mamma, we is playing'," was the reply; " we's playin' that we's growed-up HAD TO TELL z-,0:4E. ONE.—" If you" been half an hour later," she said, "I don't .)w what I should have done." "What's h• ~ened ?" he asked. "Why, Mrs. Gadding ne: .00r, has been in here with such an extrao;dir y tale, which she made me promise I would n. er breathe to a living soul, that it has seemed us if I positively couldn't wait for you to come home to tell you about it."

HE AGREED.—" Much time that might be better employed," said the advocate of spelling reform, "is taken up its the writing of foolish and unneces- sary letters." "It is indeed," was the earnest comment of the young man who had a breach of promise suit hanging over his future like a damp and dismal cloud. AFTER THAT.—A well - known university pro- fessor was lecturing to some students on hygiene some time ago, when one of the class—from the provinces—asked him how he—the student— could safeguard himself in drinking London water. The professor rather startled him by replying— " First boil it, then filter it, and, after that— drink beer." WHY HE GRUNBLED. "About the funniest guest we ever i .d," said a hotel clerk, was a solemn-looking niu who came in late one night and went to his room. An hour later he rushed back into the office as mad as a hornet. "After some time he quieted down enough to tell his troubles. "• I came here,' he declared, 'to com- mit suicide by turning on the gas, and you put me in a room lighted by electricity!' " HE (after a quarrel, much affected) : "And do —do you really mean that v,e must part, Maud ?-- She (still more affected): "I do—do, George."— He: "Never to—to meet again ?"--She : Nev. never to meet again ! "—lie: But—but suppose we should meet again by accident ?"—She : " never thought of tha-that. It is just pos-possible. You—you know where 1 gen generally take a wa- walk on Sun-day evenings ? "—He: "I do. Goo- good-bye, darling !"—She : "Goo-good-bye for— ever, Ge-Georee !" SUITING BOTH PARTIES.—Poor Wife (to hu;band, whose loud snoring keeps her awake): "Charlie, Charlie, do stop snoring. Turn over on your side." (Nudges him). Husband, only half awake, grunts, turns on his side, and continues to snore. Wife has a happy idea. Itenembers a line from an article called "How to Prevent Snoring." Gives her husband a second nudge, which elicits another grunt. "Oh, Charlie, if you'd keep your mouth shut you'd be all right." Charlie (semi-conscious) : "So would you." MARRIAGE A LOTTERY. lie looked happy enough as tie to the post-offi.:e box, set a huge bundle on !Lour, and began taking pretty square envelopes • fi,b-efroin. drooping them by two and threes in t ',ox. " BRI lot of letters," remarked the [edit:clean. " Nice day, too" " Letters !" :said the happy man. "My dear fel- low, these are not letters ; they are welding invi— tations." A stern hok ewe: over the face of the hitherto friendly policeman. "My friend," he said, "I am sorry to dist urb you, but I must do my duty. Come with me." " Ariested?" "Yes." "On what charge ? This is an outrage." " Not at all. You are advertisieg a lottery through the post. BETTING ON A CERTAINTY —A lieutenant was shooting on the rille rioge, utit tie " called " each shot as he fired, without waiting for the markers to signal the result. " You're a pretty good guesser," said the colonel. " Why don't you admit you're guessing where those shuts land ?" "I'll bet you a box of cigars," said the junior officer, "that I can call twenty shots in succession." "Taken," said the old warrior. The lieutenant fired. •4 Miss," he announced, ,ind a red flag froQ the target told that this was correct. Another shot. "Miss," declared. A third shot. "Miss again," he eaid. Fourth shot. "Fourth miss," he announced. Another shot. " Miss," again sang out the lieuenant. "Hold on there !" put in the colonel. "What are you trying to do! I thought you were going to fire at the target." "I'm trying to win my box of cigars," said the lieutenant. " Dan't fire any more," said the colonel. "They're yours."

Sir,—The following will probably be.of interest to many of the residents of Stockton Heathand to parents in particular. _

At the desire of several householders and ratepayers I have handed to the Chairman of the Parish Council a requisition (duly subscribed to as authorised by statute) asking him to convene at an early date a meeting of the parishioners in order to discuss the question of the need of the erection of a new school within the district. The necessity of a new school is based upon the following particulars. The population of Stockton Heath is increasing at a very rapid rate. At present the district has only one public school. This school although attended by over 700 children has only accommodation for a little more than 500. It is therefore very much overcrowded. This overcrowding is alleged by several parents from time to time to be a source of idleness to their children. That in addition to the school being overcrowded many parents from various causes, send their chil- dren to schools in Warrington. This is felt not only in some cases to be a hardship upon young children but also a source of considerable expense to the parents. That it is anticipated that Educational Authority in Warrington will very shortly decline to allow children who reside out of the Borough to be educated in their schools. That although it must be acknowledged thepre- sent school has in time past done a good work for the educational needs of the district, it is not now able to meet the present and future requirements of the district. That it isdesired by many in the district to have a school erected which will enable the children to be educated in all respects equal at least to the standard of other districts and thus have them efficiently equipped in this respect for their future careers in life.

The above are some of the points which are being raised and some of us sincerely hope for the sake of the children's future welfare that all sections of the com- munity, irrespective of creed or party, will work hand in hand, and subsequently either through our Parish Council or directly lodge an appeal to the Cheshire County Council (whom we understand are the Local Educational Authority) that they will at as early date as possible enquire into the educational needs of the district, subsequently cause such a school to be erected tha*he inhabitants of the district may be truly proud of.—Yours faithfully,
E. ENGLAND.

div.head: Warrington's Roman Remains.
div.p: Warrington's Roman Remains.

Sir,—An attempt is being made to discredit the Museum Committee for expending money in excavating on the site of the Roman civitas at Wilderspool and Stockton Heath. The amount so expended can always be ascertained by consulting the Borough Treasurer's account in the annual volume deposited in the Free Library. Though I have devoted the whole.of my spare time and energy during the last seven years to assisting, directing, and describing the results of these excava- tions, which have yielded what one of the highest authorities in the North of England, Professor Boyd Dawkins, in a letter to me, describes as "an important contribution to our knowledge of Roman Britain," I have been very careful not,toj&ccept any remuneration directly or indirectly for doing so. I have also pre- sented a large portion of my own private collection of Roman antiquities from the same locality to the Museum under the belief that it was the proper place of deposit andihave been accorded a vote of thanks by the Town Council,and numerous letters of thanks from the Museum Committee for such gifts. These are facts which give me a right to a hearing in justification of the outlay on digging, which I have always advocated. One of the latest and most instructive writers on. " Early Metallurgy, &c," Mr. William Gowland, F.S.A, F.C.S., writing in" Archteologia,"vol. lvi. p. 314, says it is ver3.-Isurprising that "No debris of any furnace sufficiently perfect to enable us to deduce from it its original form, has yet beeni unearthed" among the lextensive remains of thelironindustryduringthe Roman occupation of Britain.

This gentleman has been informed of the discovery of four iron smelting and purifying furnaces of the Roman period in Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co.'s field at Wilderspool in 1899 and 1900, and has since exchanged with me his papers on this interesting subject. It ought to be a source of satisfaction to the numerous iron workers of Warrington that the oldest iron furnaces in Britain or perhaps in Europe have been found in their own town. By the co-operation of Mr. P. G. Ruddock, F.1.C., the Boman system of iron manufacture has also for the first time been explained in my last report. Another original and interesting discovery made on the same ground at Wilderspeol is a seat of Roman glass-making, remains of furnaces, a clay pot containing crude glass, lumps of scum or sandiver, crude and waste glass, fragments of more than a gross of different glass vessels many beads (one of them the largest found in Britain), coloured and cut glass and a wheel for cutting glass ecc. This is the first discovery of the kind yet made in Britain, and the Warrington glass-workers ought to be interested in the discovery. Potters' kilns of the Roman period have been found in other localities, but those uncovered at Stockton Heath are among the most perfect and curious yet found, and they may still be seen by permission of the occupier of the ground, though they have been covered in by a hut. The Museum Committee cannot, however, be accused of spending money for the purpose of making these dis- coveries, which were in progress two or three years be-, fore the Museum Committoe made their first amnia' grant of £l5 in 1898. Their object in expending money was in order to secure the "finds" for the Museum for it was natural to suppose that the antiquarian societies in Manchester, Liverpool, or Chester (who were willing to undertake the work on the same terms) would ex- pect to retain the "finds "for their local museums, if they paid the money. When the ratepayers learn that only one-third of the total cost of these excavations has fallen upon the Museum Committee since 1898, they will probably con- sider the bargain a good one. A certain amount of money has always been earmarked by the Committee for the purchase of antiquities, and what better ones can be got than those belonging to their own ancient town?

The following sums were subscribed by private per- sons, principally by members of the Museum Committee viz., in 1899-1900, £l6 4s. 6d. ; 1900-1, £9 16s. 6d. ; 1901-2, £2 2s. Nothing but the expense of spade labour and the analysis of specimens has been since borne by the Committee. The cost of printing and illustrating my reports has been undertaken by the Historic' Society of Lancashire and Cheshire, which expended over £3O on illustrations alone in 1900 and initiated the excava- tions by a grant of £lO in 1898. My own labours in excavating, oleaning, and recording specimens, prapar- ing plans and drawings, and reporting have been their own reward. - -

In my opinion the Museum Committee that neglected to secure these antiquities connected with its own locality and ancient history would be as contemptible as those who seek to discredit it for doing so.—Yours, Lower Walton, Juno Ist, 1903.
THOMAS MAY.
JOSEPH PODMORE, Hairdressers_ Delegate to the Council._
P.S.—I am sending cOPies of this to the Press, so that with the Editor's kind permission, the delegates may read it before' the Council meeting.

The Licensing Compensation Question. Sir,—Mr. Longton in his reply to my letter on this subject asks me to forgive him if he suggests that my analogy of the Carriage tax and the tax on licences was a ridiculous comparison. I will forgive Mr. Longton any assertion he makes, if he will prove its truth, but until he does this I decline to accept his description of the figure used. I introduced the analogy of the Icarriagej tax, and showed wherein it was similar to the licensees' tax, but that the question of ownership, and right to compensa- tion in case of damage was different, inasmuch as the carriage was paid for by the owner, while the licensee did not buy his licencelfrom the public. Ido not think your readers are so dense as Mr. Longton would have us think he is and quite appreciate the point of simi- larity, and that of difference. Mr. Longtou takes exception to my not answering a question he puts in detail respecting a supposed case. The answer to the question depends upon the principle applicable to all. My whole letter was an answer to the question. If I can show that a licensee has no claim to compensation from the puhlic, should the magistrates decide that the licensed house as not required, then this applies all round whatever the particular circumstances maybe. Mr. Longton complains of the length of my letter, and then himself proceeds to write one of equal length largely occupied an dealing with topics that have little or nothing to do with the subject we are discussing. If with me he desires to curtail this correspondence, he will, in future, avoid the introduction of extraneous matter, and confine himself to the point at issue,namely the right of the authorities to withhold as well as to grant licenses, and in the event of such being with- held the applicant's right to compensation. Mr. Longton wanders round this issue in an aimless sort of fashion and tells us about the amount of soup, er.c., given by licensees the effect of telephone, motor cars, on lunacy, etc.' &c. It is not a matter of surprise to me to learn that licensees are kind to their customers, who are down in their luck, and often provide them ith ou p I have never looked upon those engaged in ' the trade as differing from other human beings, or of i having less 'of the milk of human kindness, but I can- not see what this has to do with the question of compensation. Let me try and bring Mr. Longton back to the point at issue. In Mr. Longton's first letter speaking of the legal aspect of the question of compensation, he said that beyond the case referred to (Sharpe v. Wakefield) , the authority was all the other way. In my reply I I , showed that the authority, instead of being the other ' way, was in strict accordance with the decision referred I to. It is a pity Mr. Longton made the statement about I the authority being all the other way, if he was I ! not prepared to produce his authorities, and make I his words good, and if he cannot make them I good, it would be more straightforward to acknowledge he was wrong, rather than to evade the point by saying: "I do not think Mr. Editor, a legal discussion would be particularly appreciated." , Mr. Longton takes me to task in speaking of "vested • Interest"while he calls it "a property, and an interest in a licence." I fail to see any difference. What Mr. Langton desires to see established as a property is nothing more or less than a vested interest, and to ob- ject to the term is mere quibbling with words. I I have no desire further to discuss the question of the legal claim if Mr. Longton abandons it. But lam in the unfortunate position of not knowing whether your correspondent still maintains his ground. in one part of his letter, where he expresses his astonishment that the trade should so long allow the law to remain as it is he seems to abandon it. But a few sentences later he speaks of magistrates exercising an"injudicial discretion. and a4tuthority warranted by no statute of the realm."' wish Mr. Longton would either stand his ground, or have courage to abandon it if untenable. If the magis- trates had no legal authority for their action Mr. Longton surely can prove it, and if this action is • illegal and the law against them, what is the necessity of calling upon the trade to exercise their power in getting the law altered? I am interesteil in Mr. Longton's plea for a continu- ance of licences because they pay £2O a year as a tax and thus save the taxpayers. Need I again remind him that before the ratepayers can congratulate themselves on any balance from such a source the consequences of intemperance have first to be liquidated. Take one phase' the crop of "drunk and disorderlies," or drunken assaults, that come up with monotonous regularity before the magisterial bench, The man or woman as a rule has injured property or person, it may be the police his wife or children. The individual is brought up by the police, imprisoned, fed, eic., at the ratepayers expense, turned out at the end of his time, often to return again and again,go through the same weary round, and finally with shattered health and character, become a burden to the public in the Workhouse. Meanwhile his wife and children have to find for themselves, getting what help they can from the rates, and swelling the number of the badly housed, clothed, and fed, with everything to drag and keep them down, forming a social and financial burden on the rest of the community. Mr. Longton does not seem to like me connecting these results with the trade. But why not face the facts if they are facts? Mr. Longton may say that these are instances of individual want of res- traint, and are not necessarily fruits of the trade. I grant this, but in my own industry if a man has an accident the owner has to pay compensation to make the loss good. These accidents are not the natural product of our manufacture. We take every means to avoid them, just as many

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.

div.head: CRICKE-I'.
div.p: CRICKE-I'.

Earlestown arranged a fixture for Saturday with Sutton, but the match was of only a second rate character, owing to the unequal strength of the teams. The Sutton men were unable to withstand the bowling of Alderson and Howarth, and they were all easily dis- posed of for 27, whilst Earlestown put on the respect- able total of 144. The fielding of the Sutton team was very smart but they were weak with the bat.
-- 1 Newton managed to make a draw with South East Manchester, on the latter's ground. Manchester batted first, and were all out for 148, whilst Newton obtained 88 for the loss of 8 wickets.
Newton, second, at home, put on 141 for 8 wickets, as against Manchester 30. The Newton second team are aoing strongly this season, and their record is likely to be an excellent one.

On Monday, Newton 2nd went to New Brighton to play an A team of the Cheshire resort. New Brighton compiled 116, but Newton had to have two innings to beat this, the total of their scores being 163. It is to be feared however that the players were more bent on pleasure than on serious cricket and perhaps this accounts for the poor show they made.

The May Queen festival on Saturday, if one may judge by the proportions of the procession and the state of the weather,should have been a gigantic success, and probably the funds of St John's Church will benefit materially. The arrangements, however, might have been very greatly improved, with very little cost to the promoters. In the procession were very many young children, who after trudging round the town in theheat and glare of the sun appeared to be almost exhausted when they arrived at the end of their journey. Sym- pathetic spectators furnished some of them with oranges, which were evidently welcome to the young- sters, but this is a duty which should have been per- formed by those responsible for the festival. Tt is hardly fair to expect the children to turn up to swell the funds of any particular place and then to be sent off at the finish empty-handed. An orange is not much, but it means a great deal to tired, hot and thirsty children. Perhaps it was an oversight. Let us hope it was so.

The walking craze has extended to Newton, but happily the cases of infection were only slight. Not very many took the disease, only about 7, and of these five called themselves a slow pack, and very well they upheld the title. Chester was their destination and al- though the distance is only about 25 miles, they occupied 31 hours in getting over it. Of course the day washot and doubtless the dust would trouble their breathing very much, and probably they needed refreshers by the way. At any rate they feel proud of their achievement, and if they didlnot perform the journey in the fastest time on record, they certainly must have broken the record for slowness.

div.head: PASSIVE RESISTANCE. Two Ministers and a Quaker to be
div.p: PASSIVE RESISTANCE. Two Ministers and a Quaker to be
Summoned.

The St. Albans School Board decided on Weinesday to refuse to pay the rate of a penny in the pound levied under the Education Act on two grounds—first, that it was illegal to make a rate not required until a period after the expiration of that for which the rate was levied, and secondly, that the money would be devoted to the support of privately managed schools. The Town Clerk had stated that the latter was not the case. The decision was arrived at on the casting vote of the chairman. The Tanbridge Wells Town Council on Wednesday,by a majority of votes, endorsed the Finance Committee's report to issue summonses against Nonconformist adherents to the policy of passive resistance to the education rate to cover the deduction. Two leading I local ministers and a prominent Quaker layman will test the question of rate recovery, and will be backed up by all Nonconformists and Liberals, who maintain that there are sixty Churchmen on the Education Com- mittee and only six Dissenters. At a meeting of the Gloucester Liberal Committee on Wednesday, under ho presidency of Sir Charles Dilke, it was decided to fight every County Council seat in Gloucester upon the education question. It was reported that similar steps were being taken and organ- ised in Somerset, Wilts and Dorset. A WIRKSWORTH MANIFESTO.

The following manifesto has been issued by the sup- porters of passive resistance at Wirksworth : " We,the members of the League, are firmly convinced that the constitutional rights and principles of civil and religious liberty, which have been for many years the birthright of every British subject, are endangered by the provisions of the Education Act, and we have there- fore banded ourselves together for the mutual support and defence of those who on religious,moral, or national grounds feel it their bounden duty to withstand the proposed encroachment. "We wish it to be clearly understood that we have no desire to separate ourselves from the general ad- ministration of law and civil order, and that we bear no to any religious communion as such. We are in full sympathy with educational progress, and our protest is simply directed against the erroneous prin- ciples embodied in the Act, viz., taxation without adequate representation and the levying of a rate upon the whole community in the interests of any particular , denomination. In pledging ourselves to passive resist- ance we desire only to vindicate principles which we regard as more important for the general welfare of the country than for our own immediate interests. "We clearly recognise and heartily accept the funda- mental principle that the State is entitled to claim from its subjects active assistance in carrying out the laws of the land, but we believe that there are grave crises in a nation's, history when good citizens may rightly deem it their duty to withhold this active co- operation. Believing that such a crises has now arisen, and being lovers of justice, liberty, and public peace, we feel ourselves in duty bound to refuse to pay that portion of the education rate which is to be used for sectarian purposes. We shall show all the respect in our power to the law of the land, abstaining from hin- dering its officers in the discharge of their duty; but active co-operation in carrying out the rating provi- sions of the Act we solemnly decline to give. "We cannot conscientiously pay rates for the main- tenance of schools in which maylegally be given teach- ing hostile to and even destructive of the Churches to which we respectively belong, and to which we owe much that is of priceless value. Such payment involves us in responsibility for the teaching given, some of which we regard as unscriptural, pernicious, and de- structive of true religion. The State ought not to compromise any of its subjects or wound their con- sciences by compelling them to pay for the propagation of opinions which they abhor. Yet the Act will com- pel some Nonconformist parents to send their children to schools, and all ratepayers to pay for these children being taught in them that their fathers' religious beliefs are false. "The Act perpetuates the imposition of religious tests upon teachers whose salaries are wholly paid from public funds. There are 16,410 head teacherships in the country, to which it is impossible for Nonconformists to get, access without violating their faith, and thus continues the unjust and mischievous supremacy of de- nominational over national interests.
"It also violates the principle of - a directly elected educational authority, with full and complete local popular control over schools entirely supported by tho State.

"The Act is national, and we cannot sever ourselves from the country as a whole. Local interests do not in- cludeall the interests involved in this struggle. The ground for fighting is the injustice of the Act, and the hour forbattle is now. "We trust that the willingness of thousands of Non- conformists to suffer loss will open the eyes of the Government to these two facts—(l) that Free Church- men are conscious of having had areal injustice inflicted upon them, and (2) that they do not intend to submit to the injustice, but to demand speedy redress." It is expected that inn few days' time a distraint will be made upon the goods of the four resisters who have been summoned already. Another demonstration will then be held.

Sankey Wire Mills were again beaten on Saturday Lymm being victorious by a margin of 13. J. Ferris and Thorpe lent valuable assistance to the winners their batting and bowling being equally good. For the Wire Mills Woodcock gave the best display with the bat his innings producing 12 runs. Cook captured no fewer than six wickets for ten runs.

Latchford Baptists were in fine form and accounted for Stretton and Appleton without difficulty. The last named eleven ran up the total of 44, and to this the Baptists had responded with 83 for the loss of only 6 wickets when play ceased. E. Wirrell (23), J. Lester (20), and J. Hallam (12), batted in capital style for the victors, whilst A. Jones (12), and J. Hoorfield (11), were the highest scorers on the other side.
By the narrow majority oE 5 runs Penketh defeated the Weston contingent. There was no tall scoring on either side W. Crosskill being the most successful batsman with 16.

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

Local cyclists gave a good account of themselves at the various sports held on Whit Monday at Sheffield Charity Tournament. A. E. Howard rode in grand style, winning the half-mile cycle handicap from the 70 yards mark in 1 minute 74-5 seconds, while he came in third in the mile bicycle after a tight finish. C. Berry figured in the half mile and threequarter mile cycle handicaps at Worksop and obtained the first position in each event somewhat easily. T. Astill took part in the one mile and three mile races at Garston cricket club sports and rode in second in each. W. Cohn had the distinction of winning the two miles bicycle handicap at Bangor. On saturday he carried off the second prize in the mile race at Bury.

Foot Racing. L. Green, of Warrington, gained the first prize in the 220 yards handicap at Sheffield Charity Tourna- ment on Saturday. He started from the 14 yards mark, and one yard was the margin by which he secured the victory. C. H. Longshaw, another War- rington sprinter, turned out at Crarston Cricket Club Sports and won the hundred yards race from the. 10 yards Mark in 10 1-5 seconds, and also the 220 yards handicap from 15 yards in 23 4-5 seconds. P. Wild- ing was second in the mile fiat race at these sports. At the Oldham police sports on Tuesday afternoon, Police Constable F. Whittaker, of the Borough Force, obtained the first prize in the 220 yards handicap, open to all police in the United Kingdom.

div.head: Angling.
div.p: Angling.

A large number of local anglers availed themselves of the opportunity of the holiday at Whitswitide to venture out in search of sport amongst various classes of fresh-water fish. Many localities, famed for fish- ing, both far and ,near were visited. But in review- ing the results of sport recorded, it cannot be said that the local.rodsters scored much success, although the climatic conditions were of a favourable char- acter. Mr. Ed. Grimshaw registered a trout of llozs. Stirs. from Farndon and Mr. Edward Kendall some half dozen small trout from Mickle Trafford. Other anglers report a few trout from various rivers in North Wales. Mr. W. H Gandy took a nice fish at Tattenball-road (Association Water). The river Bollin was not altogether in angling trim, though Messrs. Brown, jun., Cook, Green, Brown, sen., Waywell, Rathbone, B. Brown, Baker, Huddleston and Atkinson "killed" fish of varying size. Mr. Green had the best specimen of the week-end, a well-conditioned trout of 11b. 15oz. 12dr. It is inter- esting to note that a fair rise of the famed May-fly was in evidence on the river Bollin on Tuesday last. From personal observations made by the writer, the coarse fish in the lower length of this river have now completed their spawning operations, and all things considered, decent sport should be recorded after the opening date, June 15th.

Good Templars and Compensation. At the weekly session of the Temperance Mission Lodge of the Independent Order of Good Templars held on Wednesday, Bro. F. Merlin, C.T. presiding. the following resolution was proposed by Bro. E. It. Marsh, seconded by Bro. J. Drury and unanimously carried :—" That the Temperance Mission Lodge No. 1321 of the 1.0.G.T.' in regular session assembled on Wednesday the 3rd day of June, 1903, do express their regret at the action of the Right Hon. A. J. Balfour in seeking to prejudice the discretion of Justices in respect to the licenses; and protest against any proposal to provide compensation out of public funds, and that copies of this resolution be forwarded to the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition, the Lord Chancellor, the Member for the Borough, and to the local press."

A Canal Mystery. Mr. S. Brighouse held an inquest on Thursday at the Dog and Partridge Inn, 'Woolston, near Warring- ton, on the body of a male child unknown which was taken out of Woolston Canal on Tuesday about 11.30 in the morning. John Rathbone, lock keeper at -Paddington lock, said he found the body in the lock, and at once gave information to the police.—Dr. Reginald Smith, police surgeon, said he had made a post-mortem examination of the body. He found it to be that of a fully-developed male child. Decom- position was advanced, and the body must have been in the water for two or three weeks. The lungs were solid and did not contain air, and he was of the opinion that the child had not breathed nor had had a separate existence.—A verdict to the effect that the child was stillborn was returned.

div.head: NARROW ESCAPE OF A RUNCORN-BOUND VESSEL.
div.p: NARROW ESCAPE OF A RUNCORN-BOUND VESSEL.
Salvage for a Liverpool Steamer.

The Fleetwood schooner John Gibbon, bound from Runcorn to St. Mawes with a cargo of coal, had a narrow escape from destruction on the Stag Rocks, off the Lizards, during a dense fog early on Saturday. She left Runcorn on Tuesday, the 26th ult., and at 4 a.m. on Saturday, Captaia Thomas and the crew were alarmed at her grating on the rocks. There was a slight ground swell, maid the vessel was bumping heavily, threatening to shake the masts overboard. The crew took to the boats and stood by, but Captain Thomas remained on board and eventually got her clear from the rocks, when the crew rejoined the vessel. It was then found that considerable damage was done, and the water was pour- ing in so rapidly that the pumps had to be kept going. The Liverpool steamer Avon then hove in sight and towed the vessel into Falmouth Harbour. The Gibbon had a miraculous escape, as she passed between the Stag Rocks and the mainland.

div.head: LATE SPRING LANGUOR.
div.p: LATE SPRING LANGUOR.
Bile Beans and a Wonderful Case.

Scores or people suffer at this season from an ail- ment which may be called late spring languor. Those who have it lose all keenness of appetite, and take food for the mere sake of taking it and keeping "on their feet." After each meal, and especially after the mid- day meal, there is a feeling of sleepiness, depression, headache and a sense of general irritability. Sometimes it is hard to keep awake during the day, and next to impossible to get any refreshing sleep at night. This ailment may be taken as a distinct sign that the liver is torpid and sluggish, and that in turn it is exercising a baneful influence on the other organs. Constipation often occurs in this state, and very often that painful and weakening ailment, piles. Now, wherever this ailment occurs, nothing is better and brings about a cure sobner than a few timely doses of Chas. Fordo's bile beans.

Mrs. Louisa Smith, of Beaumont-road, Leyton,Essex, had this ailment for a long time. Constipation, piles, acute headache, and severe pains in the chest and shoulders after food, were all present in a very marked degree. Explaining her condition to. a Weekly Budget reporter, she said: "t actually starved myself to try and escape the pain. A short time back, I got so bad thatione night my people had to go out in the middle of the night to get me some brandy. I really thought I was going to die soon, and even sent to my friends making arrangements for my funeral, and expressing a wish to be buried by the side of my late husbsnd. I had been under the doctor for some time, but now he said the only chance of a cure was for MEI to enter the London Hospital. I dreaded that, and sug- gested waiting a day or two before deciding. In the meantime a friend asked me to try Charles Forde's bile beans and Zain-Buk Ointment for the piles. I sent fora box of beans and a box of-ointment, arid began to feel better directly I started using them. The beans worked on the system comfortably, and after each dose I felt an improvement in my condition. My appetite returned, and I could soon take my food incomfort. while the pains in my chest and back discontinued. By the time I had taken a few boxes of bile beans I was practically cured. I persevered, how- ever, both with the beans and with the ointment a little longer, until I was quite restored to health. I have never relapsed, and am to-day able to do my work with ease and pleasure." Chits. Forde's bile beans may be had from all medicine, vendors at is. Lid. or 2s. 9d. per box. Beware of sub- stitutes: and preparations. with similar sounding names.

FAIRFIELD V Sr. CYPRIAN'S LIVERPOOL.—This match was played on Fairfield' ground on Saturday last and resulted in a win for the home team. The bowlers for Fairfield were very successful; Boardman taking 4 wickets for 5 runs, and Nield 4 for 7. Nield also batted well, making a highest score of 14.

She is intended to carry iron orb from the Baltic to Rotterdam, and possesses twelve holds. Her masts, which number four- teen, are placed in two parallel rows on either side of the hatchways, and to each of the pairs are fixed two derricks, except the two end pairs, to each mast of which is fixed one derrick. Thus there are twenty-four derricks, so arranged that they can all work at once., Each of the holds is divided into two com- partments, and in this way each of the der- ricks has a twenty-fourth part of the cargo to .unload. Nowadays often only two derricks can work at a time, and the advantage of the new system is obvious. It is pleasing to note that this departure in shipbuilding is thor- oughly British and owes nothing to the Americans! PROGRESS OF THE CAPE-TO-CAIRO RAILWAY. Despite the early death of Mr. Cecil Rhodes, the pioneer and promoter of the Cape-to- Cairo Railway, which was the great dream of his life, the work goes on apace, although he is not here to superintend its progress. The railway is now getting very near to the Zam- besi, which, according to the latest advice, will be reached in a few weeks' time. A bridge is to be thrown across the river just below what is known as the "Boiling Pot," where the waters swirl through a narrow gorge, This bridge will have a span of five hundred feet, and will be a very important engineering feat. ST. HELENS. -- COLLIERY FATALITY AT HAY DOCK. An inquest was held at the Wagon Hotel, Haydock on the body of William Jones, of Crow-lane, Earles- town,who died in the Providence Hospital on Saturday from injuries received the previous day at the Newton Pit, belonging to Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. Mr. Matthews, Government inspector, Mx. Peace and Mr. Robinson (for the colliery company)were present at the inquiry.—HenryCottam, a haulage hand, who worked with deceased, said the latter came from his working to the landing, and witness went for a box for him. De- ceased sat in a manhole,. where there. was a seat. Whilst witness was jigging the journey a box came down the brow' caught witness's lamp, which was at the side and broke it. He then heard someone groaning, I and found deceased on. his face very much injured about the head. The tub was on its side.-- John Holmes, a driver, stated that he went to the land- ing with a box of coal. When he left his working place he had one scotch in the tul4 and when he got to the landing he put another in and: fastened a rope to. the. tub to lower it down. He then gave it a push down. the brow, but when he came to get hold of the rope he found it had come. off the box. He had only worked two days at this place, but had been three years in the mine. He fastened the rope on the way he had been told to do. He would not like to do his work again without assistance.—A juryman remarked that the com- pany ought to have an experienced drawer hp. a place like that.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death," and added that they were of opinion that better precaution should be taken to avoid a similar accident in future. A Birmingham lady, who was in charge of a nurse at Bromsgrove, on Wednesday escaped front her guardian and ran in front of a train. The former was killed and the latter sustained injuries in attempting a rescue. A manhas just given himself up to the police for. the murder of his wife at Walworth on Boxing Day, 1900. He states that he has had no peace since the occurrence and it has so preyed on his mind that he is now wilting to go through anything to atone.

What Will Warrington do P This month's issue of "The Burtonwood Parish Church Monthly Magazine" contains details of the progress which has been made in the scheme for the erection of a new Church and Church Hall. The following appears under the heading "What will Warrington do? ":—Our neighbouring town has not yet awakened to the fact that a new Church and Church !Hall have both to be built out here. We have waited patiently, we have waited long, for the most necessary things; the time has now come when we can wait no longer. The question is "What will Warrington do ? " Mr. Henry Lyon, Mr. Charlton Parr, and Mr. R. A. Naylor are displaying their usual generosity, and we thank them most heart ly. These are the only War- rington contributors so far, and Warrington has a large population and is a rich town. The kind un- selfish Warringtonians only need to be reminded of the claim of Burtonwood in order to extend to us that practical sympathy which we greatly long to see, both for our own sake and the sake of Warrington itself. The truest test of Parochial Spirituality is Parochial unselfishness. The claim of Burtonwood on Warring- ton is very strong; no other parish has a like claim on the neighbouring town. Burtonwood has ever been a faithful daughter, paying regula!rly to the old mother her dues, in the form of tithes and offerings. These things, if Warringtonians will consider, they will gladly and gratefully give of their substance to the supplying of our need. Will Warrington Church and Town contribute £1,000? It is not unreasonable to suggest one eighth part of the total cost of Church and Hall, and we hope it is not too great a favour to expect. An £lOO offertory would be excellent to be- gin with and would win for Warrington "the beati- tude of giving "—" it is more blessed to give than to receive."

Warrington Hairdressers' Association Eierweee. dvoe atlel pteliyeyjusctanuLo eadmisec.ou 111 cr ru n. kLeon nn ge ts os n; and the Trades Council. must not object to our placing the income coming from taxes on the trade to repairing the damage done by Sir,—l shall be obliged if you will favour our Society- intemperance, before he takes credit for relieving the by inserting the enclosed copy of letter to Mr. Stott in your Saturday's issue.—Yours sincerely, in of taxation by the licensees tax. CHARLES E. PARKER. JOSEPH PODMORE, junr., Penketh, June 4, 1903. [Copy,] 9, Rylands-street, Warrington. June 4th, 1903. Mr. F. Stott, Secretary Trades Council, Dear Sir,—As delegate to the Council for our Society, I write to tell you that on their behalf, I intend to bring before the Council, the matter of our agitation for an increase in ouriprice of work; in order to ask for the Council's help and support. This movement has grown with our Federation, and most of the branches have already established the increased prices, while others have it under con- sideration. Also the National Federation, com- posed of at present between 6,000 and 7,000 mem- bers, to which we are affiliated, is supporting and helping to extend the movement throughout the country. Had we as a trade been fully alive to the advan- tages of unity, we should not have been asking at this time of the day for an advance. While your Society (the Engineers) and all other trades have for the past 50 or 60 years been watching your own interests, we hairdressers—through apathy and unfortunate trade jealousy—have neglected our opportunities. It is only this last 10 years that any notable attempt at unity in our trade has been made, and it follows therefore that we are a long way behind other organizations both in reform of hours of work and prices for work done. It is extremely difficult to give the average earn- ings in our trade. There are three things which affect our trade considerably. Ist. The position in which a hairdresser's saloon may be placed—whether it is in a busy thorough- fare or not. 2nd. The hairdresser's own personality proving attractive to customers. 3rd. These all affect the hairdressers' income. Then again weare subjected to a great diversity in the matter of expenses in conducting our businesses. Rents vary considerably and consequently rates— together with gas bills, water rates, wear and tear, wages paid and sundry expenses. These are matters which concern each one personally. Therefore it is difficult to give an average. But from consultation and discussion among our members, I find the aver- age earnings, after deducting all necessary ex- penses is about sd. per hour. Some do better And some do worse according to the reasons given above. In the memory of the oldest hairdresser in War- rington with an experience of 60 years, there never has been an increase in the price of shaving. But the expectations of the public have increased. There is much more accommodation now compared with then. There is a marked improvement in the saloons now compared with then. And all this has not been met by any added remuneration. Alto- gether we feel justified in asking for this advance. iln doing so n Warrington, the society has not made it only a Society question but has made it a Trade question extending it to all hairdressers. It has been responded to by the trade generally with practical unanimity. We have taken every step to persuade all in the trade to join in the movement. I need not tell the Council what this means, for every society knows the trouble which is caused by a few who are obstinate. Tam glad to tell you where the branches of the Federation have established this increase, they have received most valuable support from the Local Trades Councils to which they belong and I feel con- fident that the Warrington Trades Council will not be behind others. I think the delegates will view this advance from a consistent standpoint, knowing that we are simply taking a step for a rise in wages, which they have done in years past and probably will do again in the future. I may saythat our Federation has laid down a rule that where branches have got the increased price, all members who may for any reason whatever, employ a man, must pay him a minimum wage which means an increase of several shillings per week to the man employed. In concluding this letter, let me add, I shall, all being well be present at the Council's meeting on Tuesday next when I intend asking the Council to i move a resolution supporting us n this matter and to grant the President and. Secretary power to endorse an appeal which may make if necessary— to all Trade Unionists. With best wishes yours sincerely,

Saturday's Street Collection. Sir,—The Warrington and District Christian Endeav- our Union made a 'Street Collection" last Saturday in aid of the local District Nurses Institute, when £29 10s. was collected. The members of ten Christian , Endeavour Societies were engaged in the work and fifteen stands were placed in the streets. The boxes I were kindly lent for the occasion by the Infirmary. It was noticeable that the largest amounts were collected from the poorest parts of the town where the gentle ministries of the nurses are so much needed. 6` Please miss," asked a poor old woman as she came to a stand and saw. the Red Cross "Will you read what thatsays," pointing to a bill, "'ls it for the war?" On hearing it was for the Nurses, she drew out a very shabby purse, exclaiming," For our Nurses! God bless them! I would give more if I could," and dropped two pennies into the box. Many such testimonials to the worth of the nurses were heard from the poor who gave out of their poverty in appreciation of past help received in sickness.—Yours truly, V. M. TAYLOR, Hon. Secretary, 5, Water-street; Warrington. May 28th, 1903. Stockton Heatleaducation Needs.

The quarterly session was held on Saturday at South- port representatives being present from various parts of the district, including Earlestown. Bro. J. A. Lee, D.C.T., of Liverpool presided over a large company. In his report on the position of the order throughout the district, he said that activitywprevailed,two new lodges having been opened. All the other reports were of an interesting character. Bro. E. Newman, D.S.J.T. of Earlestown, gave an excellent report of the juvenile branches. Two new Temples had been opened at Liverpool and Hindley. The following rosolution was carried :—"That this district lodge hereby protots against any attempt of the Government or ParliaiWnt to interfere with the discretionary power of justices in discharging their duties as Licensing Magistrates either by suspending or limiting such power or by providing compensation when licenses are no longer necessary for the convenience of the public ; and this district lbdge hereby pledges those present to use every legitimate effort to prevent Mr. Butcher's Compensation Bill and Sir A. Hart-Dyke's Suspensory Bill and any other measure of similar import becoming law." Next meet- ing to be at Liverpool in August. Several visitors were present from West Cheshire, Preston, and Bro. and Sister Stacey from Surrey.

On Thursday night a vestry meeting was held at Sutton, St. Helens, called by the vicar, the Rev. F. S. C. Crane, to confirm his action in placing a cross in the Parish Church—a step which has created considerable controversy. There was a crowded attendance and the proceedings were very animated. Mr. Fowles, the people's warden, appealed to the meeting to refrain from any rowdyism. The Vicar said he had received aletter from Mr. Alderman Massey, of St. Helens, suggesting that a con- ference should be held with a view of settling the matters as issue amicably. He proposed that, with a view of holding such a conference, the vestry should be adjourned for a week. This resolution wan defeated by an overwhelming majority, people shouting "Let us settle it now" and , "Down withritualism." The Vicar then proposed that a faculty be applied for to place fa cross retable, dossal cloth, &c., in St. Nisholas's Church, but an amendment proposed by Dr. Bates that a faculty be applied for to remove the cross and ornaments which the Vicar had placed in the church was carried bya great majority. The result was received with loud cheers and cries 01 "Down with. popery." FOR CLASS AND CHINA of every description try J.S.
